title: Software Development
summary: Write the code that powers the apps, platforms, and infrastructure the world runs on. The broadest and most accessible entry point into a technology career.
description: Software development covers every discipline involved in building software — frontend interfaces, backend systems, mobile apps, databases, DevOps pipelines, and the testing and tooling that keeps it all working. You can enter through self-study and a portfolio, a bootcamp, a computer science degree, or by transitioning from an adjacent technical role. The unifying skill is the ability to write code that solves real problems reliably — everything else (frameworks, languages, tools) is context that changes over time. The field spans every industry: software developers are as needed in healthcare and agriculture as they are in technology companies.
keySkills: Writing clean, readable, and maintainable code in at least one language
Understanding how the web works: HTTP, APIs, browsers, and servers
Using version control with Git for collaborative development
Debugging and reasoning about code systematically when things break
Reading documentation and learning new frameworks and tools independently
Translating a real problem into a software solution that actually works
opportunities: Software engineer across every industry sector
Full-stack, frontend, backend, or mobile developer at product companies
Developer at startups, agencies, enterprises, and government digital teams
Freelance or contract developer working across multiple clients
Technical co-founder building a software product
Open-source contributor building publicly available tools

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the landscape — frontend, backend, mobile, full-stack, and emerging areas. Pick one direction and one language. Starting broad and switching constantly is the most common way to waste the first six months.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation Building
journeyPhases.focus: Learn your chosen language and build real projects with it — not exercises, actual apps with users or real problems. Understand version control, debugging, and how to read documentation and error messages.

journeyPhases.name: Specialization and Entry
journeyPhases.focus: Choose a specialization and build a portfolio of 2–3 projects that demonstrate it. Start applying. The first role is the hardest to get — after that, demonstrated production experience accelerates everything.

title: AI and Data
summary: Build intelligent systems, extract insight from data, and engineer the infrastructure that makes machine learning real in production. The fastest-moving and most commercially impactful field in technology.
description: The AI and data field covers everything from building and training machine learning models to engineering the pipelines that feed them, analyzing the outputs they produce, and designing the products they power. It spans data analysis (turning data into decisions), data engineering (building the infrastructure that makes data available), data science (modeling and insight), machine learning engineering (building and deploying models), and prompt engineering (designing the inputs to language models). Entry is possible from a self-taught path with strong programming and mathematics skills, or from a degree in statistics, computer science, or a related discipline. The field rewards people who combine technical rigor with genuine intellectual curiosity about what data actually means.
keySkills: Writing SQL and Python for data manipulation and analysis
Applying statistical reasoning to real-world data problems
Understanding how machine learning models work at a conceptual level
Building and evaluating models or pipelines end-to-end
Communicating data findings and model behavior to non-technical audiences
Thinking critically about what data reveals and what it hides
opportunities: Data analyst, data scientist, or ML engineer across all industries
Prompt engineer or AI product specialist at AI-first companies
Data engineer building pipelines and infrastructure at scale
Research scientist at AI labs and academic institutions
Analytics engineer at data-driven product companies
AI consultant advising organizations on data and intelligence strategy

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the difference between data analysis, data science, data engineering, ML engineering, and AI product roles. Pick the direction that matches your actual skills and interests — they require significantly different foundations.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation Building
journeyPhases.focus: Build Python and SQL fluency alongside statistics fundamentals. Work through real datasets on real problems. Every direction in this field requires these foundations before anything else.

journeyPhases.name: Specialization and Entry
journeyPhases.focus: Specialize into your chosen direction and build portfolio projects that demonstrate end-to-end capability. Apply for analyst, junior data scientist, or ML engineer roles depending on your path.

title: Infrastructure and Security
summary: Keep software running reliably, securely, and at scale. The discipline that separates production systems from demos — and the foundation that every other technology role depends on.
description: Infrastructure and security covers DevOps and platform engineering, cloud architecture, cybersecurity, IT systems administration, and embedded systems. These roles manage the systems that software runs on rather than the software itself — ensuring services stay available, secure, and cost-efficient under real-world conditions. Entry into this field is often through IT support and systems administration at the junior level, then progression into cloud, DevOps, or security as skills develop. Certifications (AWS, CompTIA, Cisco) are the primary credential pathway; degrees are common but not mandatory. This field tends to attract people who are naturally systematic, calm under operational pressure, and genuinely curious about how systems fail.
keySkills: Understanding networking fundamentals: TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, and firewalls
Working with Linux command line and scripting in Bash or Python
Operating cloud platforms and understanding core services on AWS, GCP, or Azure
Thinking about failure modes — what breaks, when, and how to respond
Managing configuration and infrastructure as code
Understanding security principles: least privilege, encryption, and threat modeling
opportunities: Systems administrator, IT engineer, or DevOps engineer
Cloud architect or platform engineer at technology companies
Cybersecurity analyst or penetration tester
Site reliability engineer managing large-scale production systems
Embedded systems or IoT engineer at hardware companies
Security engineer protecting applications and infrastructure

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the spectrum from IT support through DevOps to cybersecurity. Each specialization requires different foundations — decide whether you are drawn to systems operations, cloud and deployment, or security before choosing a starting point.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation Building
journeyPhases.focus: Learn Linux, networking fundamentals, and one cloud platform. Start with CompTIA A+ or Network+ if IT administration is your entry, AWS Cloud Practitioner if cloud is your direction, or Security+ if security is your focus.

journeyPhases.name: Specialization and Entry
journeyPhases.focus: Earn a specialist certification and build hands-on lab work in your chosen area. Apply for help desk, junior DevOps, SOC analyst, or junior sysadmin roles as your entry point into the field.

title: Product and Design
summary: Define what gets built, shape how it looks, and make sure it actually works for real people. The discipline that connects user needs to engineering reality.
description: Product and design covers the roles responsible for what software does and how it feels to use — product managers who define direction and priorities, UI/UX designers who create interfaces and interactions, AI product managers who work specifically with intelligent systems, technical writers who make products understandable, and QA engineers who ensure they work correctly. These roles sit between users and engineers, translating between human needs and technical implementation. Entry is possible from almost any background — what matters most is the ability to understand both the problem and the constraints of building a solution. Many product and design professionals come from engineering, psychology, business, or writing backgrounds.
keySkills: Understanding how software is built and what is technically feasible to implement
Conducting user research and translating findings into concrete design or product decisions
Communicating clearly between technical and non-technical team members
Thinking systematically about user flows, edge cases, and failure states
Defining and measuring success for a feature or product decision
Iterating based on evidence rather than assumption or personal preference
opportunities: Product manager or associate PM at technology companies
UX or product designer at digital agencies and product startups
Technical writer or content designer at developer-focused companies
QA engineer on software development teams
AI product manager at LLM-powered product companies
Design system specialist at large technology organizations

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the distinctions between product management, UX design, research, and QA. These roles are often confused but require genuinely different skills and personalities. Shadow or interview people in each role before choosing your direction.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation Building
journeyPhases.focus: For design: build Figma skills and a portfolio. For PM: understand how software is built and practice writing product specs. For QA: learn test automation. In every case, get into a real product environment as quickly as possible.

journeyPhases.name: Specialization and Entry
journeyPhases.focus: Build portfolio work or case studies that demonstrate your specific discipline. Apply for junior roles — APM programs for PM, junior designer for UX, QA engineer for testing. The first product role accelerates learning faster than any preparation.

title: Emerging Technology
summary: The frontier of what software and hardware can do. Robotics, immersive environments, decentralized systems, and the technologies that don't fully exist yet but are defining the next decade.
description: Emerging technology covers the technology disciplines that are either newly viable or rapidly evolving — game development, robotics engineering, drone and UAV systems, mental health technology, and fintech development. These fields share a common characteristic: they combine core software engineering with domain-specific knowledge that is not yet well-established or widely taught. Robotics requires control theory and hardware integration; fintech requires financial system knowledge and compliance understanding; mental health technology requires sensitivity to clinical and ethical constraints. Entry typically requires strong foundational software or engineering skills plus deliberate investment in the domain-specific knowledge layer that makes each specialization distinct.
keySkills: Strong foundational software or hardware engineering skills transferable across domains
Domain-specific knowledge in the area you are targeting (finance, health, robotics, gaming)
Comfort working in fields where documentation and best practices are still being established
Ability to learn from communities, open-source projects, and practitioners rather than textbooks
Understanding regulatory and ethical constraints relevant to your specific domain
Prototyping and experimenting rapidly in environments where nothing is fully figured out yet
opportunities: Game developer at indie or AAA studios
Robotics or automation engineer at industrial or commercial robotics companies
Drone systems engineer or operator at survey, agriculture, or defense companies
Fintech engineer at digital banks, payment companies, or financial infrastructure startups
Developer or PM building mental health and digital therapeutics products
Space technology engineer at commercial launch or satellite companies

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Identify which emerging technology specialization genuinely interests you — interest matters more here than in mature fields because there is less structured training. Understand what foundational engineering skills each direction requires.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation Building
journeyPhases.focus: Build the core technical foundation for your target specialization — game engine skills for game development, embedded systems for robotics, backend and financial APIs for fintech. Domain knowledge comes after foundational competence.

journeyPhases.name: Specialization and Entry
journeyPhases.focus: Build portfolio work in your specific domain. Emerging fields are relationship-driven — communities, forums, open-source projects, and game jams provide entry points that traditional application processes often do not.

title: Clinical Medicine
summary: Direct patient care — diagnosis, treatment, and the relationship at the heart of medicine. The longest training path in healthcare and among the most consequential careers in any field.
description: Clinical medicine covers all the healthcare professions that provide direct diagnostic and treatment services to patients — doctors, pharmacists, dentists, optometrists, veterinarians, emergency medical practitioners, and midwives. Every path in this field requires a degree, a supervised clinical training period, and a government-issued license to practice independently. The training is long, rigorous, and ethically serious — because the decisions you make directly affect people's health and lives. Clinical medicine rewards people who combine intellectual rigor with genuine human empathy, the ability to function well under uncertainty, and the communication skills to build trust with patients who are frightened and vulnerable.
keySkills: Systematic clinical reasoning and diagnostic problem-solving under uncertainty
Performing clinical examinations, procedures, and assessments relevant to your specialty
Communicating complex medical information clearly to patients and families
Recognizing the limits of your competence and escalating when required
Managing multiple patients with different levels of acuity simultaneously
Maintaining accurate clinical records and working within regulatory frameworks
opportunities: Physician or GP in primary care or hospital settings
Pharmacist in community, hospital, or pharmaceutical industry roles
Dentist in private or public practice
Optometrist in clinical or community settings
Veterinarian in companion animal, agricultural, or research roles
Paramedic or emergency medical practitioner in pre-hospital care
verificationNote: All clinical medicine pathways require country-specific registration and licensing; qualification requirements, board examinations, and supervised training periods vary significantly by profession and region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Direction
journeyPhases.focus: Research the specific clinical profession you are targeting — the training, the day-to-day reality, and the licensing requirements in your country. Gain clinical shadowing or work experience before applying. Commitment to this field is significant; confirmation of fit is essential.

journeyPhases.name: Degree and Clinical Training
journeyPhases.focus: Complete your professional degree with integrated clinical placements. Pass licensing examinations required for registration. The clinical placement phases are as important as the academic content — this is where clinical judgment develops.

journeyPhases.name: Specialization and Registration
journeyPhases.focus: Complete post-graduate supervised practice required for full registration. Choose a specialization if applicable. Registration grants independent practice rights. Most clinical careers then develop through continuing professional development and experience.

title: Nursing and Allied Health
summary: The clinical professionals working closest to patients every day — from bedside nursing to rehabilitation, imaging, nutrition, and speech therapy. Essential, regulated, and in demand everywhere.
description: Nursing and allied health covers the large group of regulated clinical professions that deliver direct patient care alongside doctors — nurses, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, radiographers, dietitians, and speech-language pathologists. These roles are the largest workforce in healthcare and the ones patients most frequently interact with. Each requires a degree and national registration. The work is physically and emotionally demanding, clinically skilled, and deeply human — you work with people at their most vulnerable over extended periods. Allied health professionals in particular are among the most underrecognized contributors to patient recovery — physiotherapy, speech therapy, and occupational therapy often determine whether a patient regains independence or not.
keySkills: Direct patient assessment, monitoring, and clinical intervention in your specialty
Building therapeutic relationships with patients across extended recovery periods
Working within multidisciplinary clinical teams with clear role boundaries
Documenting patient care accurately and maintaining clinical records
Recognizing deterioration and escalating concerns through appropriate channels
Applying evidence-based practice to clinical decision-making in your specialty
opportunities: Registered nurse across all specialties and healthcare settings
Physiotherapist in hospital, community, or private practice
Occupational therapist in rehabilitation, mental health, or community settings
Radiographer in diagnostic imaging departments
Dietitian in clinical, community, or sports nutrition settings
Speech-language pathologist in pediatric, neurological, or voice specializations
verificationNote: All nursing and allied health professions require country-specific registration; licensing examinations, clinical placement requirements, and scope of practice vary by profession and region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Direction
journeyPhases.focus: Research the specific allied health profession you are drawn to — each requires different training and offers a different daily reality. Get work or volunteer experience in a relevant clinical setting before applying to confirm genuine fit.

journeyPhases.name: Degree and Placements
journeyPhases.focus: Complete your professional degree with mandatory clinical placements in your specialty. The placements are where clinical competence develops — academic study provides the framework, clinical practice provides the skill.

journeyPhases.name: Registration and Entry
journeyPhases.focus: Complete registration requirements and any induction period for newly qualified practitioners. Begin developing clinical confidence and a specialty focus. Continuing professional development and additional qualifications drive long-term career progression.

title: Mental Health and Psychiatry
summary: The professionals who treat the mind — through therapy, medication, or structured support. Stigma is decreasing, demand is growing, and the shortage of qualified practitioners has never been more acute.
description: Mental health and psychiatry covers the spectrum of clinical and counseling professions focused on psychological and psychiatric wellbeing — from addiction and mental health counselors who provide structured support, through clinical psychologists who deliver evidence-based therapy, to psychiatrists who diagnose and treat mental illness with the full scope of medical knowledge including medication. The paths differ enormously in training length and clinical scope — counseling can be entered in 2–3 years; psychiatry requires medical school plus specialist training totaling over a decade. What unifies the field is the combination of clinical skill and genuine human empathy, and the recognition that mental health disorders are as real and as treatable as physical ones.
keySkills: Building therapeutic alliances with people experiencing significant psychological distress
Applying evidence-based therapeutic or psychiatric interventions within your clinical scope
Assessing and managing risk of self-harm, suicide, and harm to others
Working within the regulatory and ethical frameworks governing your profession
Engaging in clinical supervision as a mandatory professional practice
Communicating effectively with multidisciplinary mental health and medical teams
opportunities: Counselor or therapist in schools, GP practices, community settings, or private practice
Clinical psychologist in NHS, hospital, forensic, or private settings
Psychiatrist in community, inpatient, child and adolescent, or forensic settings
Mental health nurse in crisis, inpatient, or community mental health teams
Addiction specialist at residential or outpatient treatment centers
Mental health academic combining research and clinical practice
verificationNote: Mental health professions require country-specific registration and licensing; training requirements and scope of practice vary significantly by profession and region — verify before starting any program.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Direction
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the distinction between counseling, psychology, and psychiatry — the training paths, scopes of practice, and day-to-day realities are fundamentally different. Gain experience in a mental health setting before committing to a training route.

journeyPhases.name: Training and Qualification
journeyPhases.focus: Complete the training required for your chosen role. Counseling and psychotherapy diplomas: 2–3 years. Clinical psychology doctorate: 6–9 years total. Psychiatry: medical school plus specialist training of 10–14 years. Supervised clinical hours are mandatory for all routes.

journeyPhases.name: Registration and Practice
journeyPhases.focus: Complete registration requirements, accumulate required supervised practice hours, and begin independent or supervised practice. Personal therapy during training is required or strongly recommended in most mental health professions.

title: Biomedical and Research
summary: The laboratory, research, and technology infrastructure that makes modern medicine possible. Without this field, clinical decisions cannot be made, drugs cannot be developed, and medical devices cannot be built.
description: Biomedical and research covers the scientific and technical professions that underpin clinical medicine without directly treating patients — biomedical scientists who run diagnostic laboratories, neuroscientists who study the brain, public health professionals who protect entire populations, biomedical engineers who design medical devices, and health informaticians who connect clinical knowledge with technology. These roles are where medicine meets science, engineering, and technology. Most require degree-level qualifications; research and senior positions typically expect postgraduate study. This field suits people who are motivated by the mechanisms behind medicine rather than direct patient contact.
keySkills: Applying scientific and analytical methods relevant to your specific biomedical discipline
Designing and conducting research with appropriate controls and statistical methods
Working with biological samples, clinical data, or medical technology with precision and safety
Interpreting findings in the context of clinical or public health implications
Contributing to research publications, reports, or regulatory documentation
Working within quality management and regulatory standards relevant to your setting
opportunities: Biomedical scientist in hospital diagnostic or reference laboratories
Neuroscientist at pharmaceutical companies or research institutions
Public health analyst or epidemiologist at government agencies or NGOs
Biomedical engineer at medical device design and manufacturing companies
Health informatics specialist at hospital systems or digital health companies
Research scientist at academic medical centers or biotechnology companies

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Direction
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the distinct roles within biomedical and research — laboratory science, public health, device engineering, and informatics require different foundational skills. Identify which direction aligns with your interests and strengths.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Complete a degree in biomedical science, neuroscience, public health, biomedical engineering, or health informatics. Develop laboratory or analytical skills through practical modules. Consider whether postgraduate study is required for your target role.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Specialization
journeyPhases.focus: Enter a graduate role in your chosen area. A master's or PhD is typically required for research-track careers. For applied roles (device engineering, informatics, lab science), undergraduate degree plus professional accreditation is often sufficient.

title: Strategy and Consulting
summary: Shape what organizations do and how they do it. The highest-leverage thinking roles in business — where rigorous analysis meets real organizational change.
description: Strategy and consulting covers the roles responsible for defining organizational direction and solving complex business problems — business analysts, management consultants, project managers, and sustainability advisors. These roles all require the ability to frame problems clearly, analyze them rigorously, and communicate findings in ways that drive decisions. Entry is possible from almost any degree background; what matters is analytical ability, clear writing, and the intellectual flexibility to work across different industries and problem types. Management consulting attracts people who want variety and exposure to many types of organizations; internal strategy roles attract those who prefer depth in one business.
keySkills: Structuring ambiguous problems into clear analytical frameworks
Building business cases and financial models that withstand scrutiny
Communicating complex analysis simply and persuasively to senior stakeholders
Managing multiple workstreams simultaneously under deadline pressure
Facilitating workshops and driving alignment across different organizational functions
Identifying root causes rather than symptoms in business performance problems
opportunities: Management consultant at strategy or Big 4 consulting firms
Business analyst at financial services, government, or technology organizations
Project manager across all industries and sectors
Internal strategy analyst at large corporations
Sustainability or ESG consultant at advisory firms
Transformation program manager at organizations undergoing significant change

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the distinctions between consulting, business analysis, project management, and strategy roles — they overlap but require different skills and have different career trajectories. Identify which type of problem-solving most interests you.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation Building
journeyPhases.focus: Develop structured thinking, financial modeling, and clear written communication. Business analysis certifications (ECBA) and project management credentials (CAPM, PMP) provide structured entry paths with clear milestones.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Specialization
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for analyst or junior consultant roles. Sector knowledge in finance, healthcare, technology, or government significantly improves competitiveness. The first consulting role builds the experience base for everything that follows.

title: Marketing and Growth
summary: Drive how people discover, feel about, and choose the things that matter to them. Part science, part creativity — and behind every brand that actually connects with its audience.
description: Marketing and growth covers every discipline involved in building awareness, desire, and demand for products, services, and organizations — brand strategy, digital marketing, e-commerce, sales, and content creation. The field is highly varied: brand marketers work on identity and perception; performance marketers optimize acquisition and conversion; product marketers launch features and position them to specific audiences; sales professionals convert interest into revenue. The common thread is understanding people — what they want, what they believe, and what drives their decisions. Entry is accessible from many backgrounds; demonstrated results matter more than qualifications in most areas of this field.
keySkills: Understanding customer behavior, segmentation, and buyer journey dynamics
Running and measuring marketing campaigns across digital and traditional channels
Writing persuasively and clearly for different audiences and contexts
Analyzing marketing performance data and making decisions based on what it shows
Building and managing commercial relationships with clients or customers
Thinking about brand perception and how organizational behavior creates or destroys trust
opportunities: Marketing manager or brand strategist at consumer or B2B companies
Digital marketing specialist or performance marketer
Sales development representative or account executive at software companies
E-commerce manager at retail or DTC brands
Social media and content creator for brands or independently
Growth marketer at startups optimizing acquisition and retention

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the breadth of marketing — brand, digital, product, content, and sales are meaningfully different. Identify which combination of creativity and analysis appeals to you and which industry contexts interest you most.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation Building
journeyPhases.focus: Build hands-on skills in your chosen area. For digital: run real campaigns with real accounts. For brand: develop portfolio projects. For sales: take any role that puts you in front of prospects and teaches you how to handle objections.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Specialization
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for roles where you can demonstrate results, not just knowledge. Marketing is a performance-based field — what you have done and the numbers it produced are more persuasive than qualifications in almost every case.

title: Operations and Logistics
summary: Keep the systems of commerce functioning. Behind every on-time delivery, every well-run business, and every product that arrives where it should be is someone who made operations work.
description: Operations and logistics covers the roles that make organizations actually function — supply chain managers who move goods across the globe, logistics coordinators who manage the movement from warehouse to doorstep, real estate professionals who handle property as a business asset, and sales and BD teams who bring in the revenue that funds everything else. These roles are less visible than strategy or marketing but often more consequential — when operations fail, everything else stops. The field rewards people who are systematic, calm under pressure, commercially aware, and genuinely interested in how complex systems can be made to run more reliably and efficiently.
keySkills: Analyzing operational systems and identifying inefficiencies, bottlenecks, and failure points
Managing supplier and partner relationships under commercial and time pressure
Using ERP, WMS, or logistics platforms to manage and track operations data
Negotiating contracts and commercial terms with counterparties effectively
Planning capacity, inventory, and resource requirements against variable demand
Communicating operational performance clearly to internal stakeholders
opportunities: Supply chain analyst or manager at manufacturing or retail companies
Logistics coordinator or operations manager at 3PL or e-commerce companies
Procurement manager at corporate organizations
Real estate investment analyst or asset manager
Sales manager or business development director
Operations director at scale-up companies building commercial systems from scratch

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the range from supply chain and logistics through to commercial operations and real estate. These specializations share operational thinking but apply it in different contexts. Identify which commercial environment most appeals to you.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation Building
journeyPhases.focus: Learn the fundamentals of your chosen area — supply chain certifications (APICS), Lean and Six Sigma basics for manufacturing, or real estate market knowledge for property roles. Get into operational environments as early as possible.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Specialization
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for coordinator or analyst roles in your target area. Operations careers are built through demonstrated performance and accumulated domain knowledge — the first operational role provides the foundation for everything that follows.

title: Entrepreneurship
summary: Build something from nothing. The most uncertain, most personal, and potentially most impactful path in business — and one that cannot be learned without doing it.
description: Entrepreneurship covers the full range of paths for people who want to build and run their own businesses rather than work within existing organizations — from founding a venture-backed technology startup to building a bootstrapped e-commerce business. The field does not have a clear credential path because the primary requirement is building something that works, not passing any examination. What determines success is the combination of market insight, execution speed, resilience through failure, and the ability to attract the customers, talent, and capital a growing business needs. Most entrepreneurs work in adjacent roles first — as employees who learn how businesses work before attempting to build one — though some go directly from education to founding.
keySkills: Identifying genuine market opportunities through observation and customer research
Building and launching a product or service quickly enough to learn before running out of resources
Acquiring first customers without a budget using direct outreach and referrals
Managing a limited-resource environment where every decision has a cost
Learning from failure quickly and adjusting course without losing momentum
Making sound decisions about hiring, capital, and direction under significant uncertainty
opportunities: Technology startup founder building a venture-backed or bootstrapped software company
E-commerce founder selling products through digital channels
Service business owner in creative, consulting, trades, or professional services
Social entrepreneur building a business around a social or environmental mission
Solopreneur building a portfolio of revenue streams as an independent operator
Intrapreneur leading internal ventures within a larger organization

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the distinct paths within entrepreneurship — technology startups, e-commerce, service businesses, and social enterprise have different capital requirements, risk profiles, and skill demands. Build a valuable skill before building a business around it.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation Building
journeyPhases.focus: Either work in a startup or small business to understand how one operates, or start building something small immediately. The best business education is attempting to get a first paying customer in the real world.

journeyPhases.name: Building and Iteration
journeyPhases.focus: Build, launch, learn, and adjust. The goal is to reach product-market fit — a condition where customers consistently find enough value that they return, refer, and pay. Everything before that is hypothesis testing.

title: People and Organisation
summary: Build and protect the culture and people of an organization. Strategy, empathy, and genuinely difficult decisions — the function that determines whether talented people stay or leave.
description: People and organization covers the human resources and organizational development functions that recruit, develop, and retain the talent that makes organizations work. HR professionals manage everything from hiring processes and employment law compliance to performance management, compensation design, and organizational culture. At senior levels, the function is genuinely strategic — CHROs shape how organizations are structured, how decisions are made, and what kind of place a company is to work. Entry into HR is accessible from many backgrounds — people who have studied psychology, business, law, or sociology all enter successfully — and certification pathways (CIPD, SHRM) provide structured routes for those coming from non-HR backgrounds.
keySkills: Managing end-to-end hiring processes from job design through offer and onboarding
Understanding employment law and applying it to real employee relations situations
Building people systems: performance frameworks, compensation structures, and career paths
Handling sensitive employee situations with consistency, fairness, and appropriate confidentiality
Advising managers on people decisions that are legally sound and commercially sensible
Measuring organizational health through engagement data and retention metrics
opportunities: HR generalist or people operations manager at growing companies
Talent acquisition specialist managing hiring at scale
HR business partner embedded in specific business units
Learning and development specialist designing training programs
Compensation and benefits analyst at large enterprises
Chief People Officer or HR director at companies building organizational capability

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the range of HR specializations — generalist, talent acquisition, L&D, compensation, and HRBP. The work is more legally and commercially complex than its reputation suggests. Research employment law basics in your country before starting.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation Building
journeyPhases.focus: Pursue a CIPD Level 3 (UK) or SHRM-CP (US) qualification or equivalent. Get into any HR coordinator or recruiting role — working with real people situations is how judgment develops, not coursework.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Specialization
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for HR coordinator, recruiter, or people ops roles at companies actively building their people function. Early specialization in talent acquisition is a common and accessible starting path.

title: Investment and Markets
summary: Analyze, price, and move capital at the intersection of companies, markets, and high-stakes strategy. Where financial rigor and commercial judgment meet under significant time pressure.
description: Investment and markets covers the financial professionals who analyze and transact on capital markets — investment bankers who advise on M&A and capital raising, financial analysts who evaluate performance and drive investment decisions, and actuaries who quantify risk mathematically. These roles share a foundation of financial analysis, modeling, and the ability to work under significant commercial pressure. Entry typically requires a strong quantitative degree and, for the most competitive roles, graduate performance at a target university or institution. The CFA designation is the most widely recognized professional credential across investment roles and significantly improves access to senior positions.
keySkills: Building and interpreting financial models including three-statement and DCF analysis
Evaluating company performance using financial statement analysis and ratio analysis
Understanding capital markets — equity, fixed income, derivatives, and structured products
Applying quantitative methods to investment decision-making and risk assessment
Communicating complex financial analysis clearly to clients and senior colleagues
Working at the intersection of mathematics, commercial judgment, and market awareness
opportunities: Investment banking analyst at bulge-bracket or boutique banks
Financial analyst in corporate FP&A or equity research
Actuarial trainee at insurance companies or consulting firms
Quantitative analyst at hedge funds or asset managers
Private equity analyst after banking experience
Credit analyst at commercial or investment banks

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Direction
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the distinct roles within investment and markets — banking, research, asset management, and actuarial science have different day-to-day realities and career trajectories. Build financial modeling basics before applying.

journeyPhases.name: Degree and Credentialing
journeyPhases.focus: Study finance, economics, or mathematics. Pursue internships in your target area — especially for investment banking, where the summer internship is the primary hiring pipeline. Begin CFA preparation if targeting investment roles.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Credential
journeyPhases.focus: Enter as a graduate analyst. Pursue professional credentials (CFA, actuarial exams) alongside work. The credential pathway in these fields takes years but significantly expands career options and compensation.

title: Financial Planning and Advisory
summary: Help individuals and families build financial security across a lifetime. Where technical financial expertise meets the most personal professional relationships in any field.
description: Financial planning and advisory covers the professionals who help individuals, families, and organizations plan for the future financially — managing savings, investments, tax, pensions, insurance, and estate planning. This field is fundamentally about long-term relationships built on trust. Clients return year after year because they trust their adviser understands their goals and is acting in their interest. The regulatory landscape varies enormously by country — most jurisdictions require licensing before you can give financial advice — but the core skill set is consistent: technical financial knowledge combined with excellent interpersonal communication. Fee-based advisory models are increasingly replacing commission-based ones, which has improved the quality and independence of advice.
keySkills: Building comprehensive financial plans across savings, investment, tax, pension, and protection
Explaining complex financial concepts and market risks clearly to non-specialist clients
Navigating regulatory requirements for financial advice suitability and disclosure
Managing client relationships through market downturns and emotionally charged financial decisions
Constructing investment portfolios aligned to specific client goals and risk profiles
Understanding the tax and estate planning implications of financial decisions
opportunities: Independent financial adviser (IFA) in private practice
Wealth manager at a private bank or wealth management firm
Financial planner at a chartered financial planning organization
Retirement and pension specialist at an insurance or investment company
Financial coach working with younger clients on financial foundations
Digital financial adviser at a robo-advice or fintech platform
verificationNote: Financial advice practice requires country-specific licensing and registration; qualification requirements and regulatory oversight vary significantly by region.

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the regulatory framework for financial advice in your country. Research the qualification pathway — CFP, CII Diploma, or equivalent — and understand what activities you can and cannot do before licensing.

journeyPhases.name: Qualification and Training
journeyPhases.focus: Complete required professional qualifications while working in a support or paraplanning role at a financial planning firm. Develop technical knowledge of the planning tools and products you will use with clients.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Practice
journeyPhases.focus: Obtain licensing, begin advising clients under supervision, and start building your client book. The most valuable asset in this field is a trusted client relationship — every professional decision should protect and grow that trust.

title: Risk and Insurance
summary: Quantify, price, and manage uncertainty. The mathematical and commercial backbone of financial stability — and a field that matters most when everything else goes wrong.
description: Risk and insurance covers the professionals who help organizations understand and financially protect against uncertainty — underwriters who price and accept risk for insurers, brokers who place risk in the market for clients, and enterprise risk managers who build frameworks to identify and mitigate the risks their organizations face. The field is more analytically rigorous than its reputation suggests: pricing complex insurance risks requires sophisticated modeling; enterprise risk management requires deep understanding of how organizations fail. Entry is accessible through insurance graduate programs, which offer structured training across the industry. The Lloyd's of London market and specialty insurance sector are particularly well-regarded entry points for those targeting international careers.
keySkills: Analyzing risk data to price insurance premiums or quantify organizational exposures
Understanding insurance contract terms, policy wordings, and coverage interpretation
Applying risk management frameworks to assess and mitigate organizational risk
Building and managing relationships with insurers, brokers, and risk management stakeholders
Modeling catastrophe and operational risk scenarios for insurance and reinsurance purposes
Navigating regulatory and compliance requirements in insurance and risk management
opportunities: Underwriter at an insurance company or Lloyd's syndicate
Insurance broker placing commercial risks for corporate clients
Enterprise risk manager at a large corporation
Catastrophe risk analyst modeling natural disaster and climate risk
Claims manager assessing and settling insurance claims
Risk consultant advising organizations on risk management strategy
verificationNote: Insurance sales and advisory roles require country-specific licensing in most regions; regulatory requirements vary by role type and jurisdiction.

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the insurance and risk ecosystem — the distinction between underwriting, broking, claims, and risk management, and how they connect. Research graduate insurance programs which provide the most structured entry into the field.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation and Training
journeyPhases.focus: Enter the field through a graduate program or junior role. Begin professional qualification — CII (UK), CPCU (US), or equivalent. Learn the technical language of risk and insurance alongside commercial relationship skills.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Specialization
journeyPhases.focus: Develop expertise in one class of insurance or risk management area. Specialty markets and niche classes (cyber, marine, D&O) often offer faster career progression than mainstream personal lines.

title: Visual Design
summary: Shape how things look and how that appearance communicates meaning. Every brand, interface, image, and illustration that has ever caught your attention was made by a visual designer.
description: Visual design covers all the creative disciplines concerned with visual communication — graphic design, illustration and concept art, animation and motion graphics, photography, UX/UI research, and fashion design. What unifies them is the application of visual thinking to solve communication problems: how do you make this clear, beautiful, and emotionally resonant? Entry into visual design is primarily portfolio-based — employers care what you can make, not what you studied. This makes it one of the most accessible creative fields to enter from a self-taught background, but also one where the bar is high because the portfolio quality of applicants is usually directly visible. Specialization matters — being a strong graphic designer is not the same as being a strong illustrator or motion designer, even though all three fall under the same broad label.
keySkills: Applying visual design principles: typography, color, hierarchy, composition, and contrast
Working in relevant digital tools (Figma, Adobe Creative Suite, Procreate) at a professional standard
Translating a brief or problem into a visual response that communicates effectively
Iterating on design work based on feedback without losing the original intent
Building and presenting a coherent body of work that demonstrates your visual perspective
Understanding the context your design will live in — screen, print, motion, or physical medium
opportunities: Graphic designer at agencies, brands, or in-house creative teams
Illustrator for editorial, publishing, gaming, and brand clients
Motion designer for advertising, broadcast, and digital content
Photographer for commercial, editorial, or documentary contexts
UX researcher applying visual and behavioral analysis to product design
Fashion designer in commercial, luxury, or sustainable fashion sectors

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the distinct visual disciplines — graphic design, illustration, motion, photography, and fashion all require different skills and tools. Pick one and go deep rather than starting broad across all of them simultaneously.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Build fundamental skills in your chosen discipline. Make real work — not exercises. Study what makes strong work in your specific area analytically. Seek feedback from practicing professionals rather than just personal networks.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio Polish
journeyPhases.focus: Curate a focused portfolio of 4–6 strong pieces and publish it. Apply for junior roles or freelance work. Visual design is almost entirely portfolio-driven — a strong body of work opens more doors than any degree.

title: Media and Production
summary: Create the content that fills screens, speakers, and feeds. Film, music, audio, games, and the channels between — the field that shapes how culture actually feels.
description: Media and production covers all the disciplines involved in creating audio-visual content — film and video production, music production, sound design and audio engineering, podcast production, social media content creation, and game design. These disciplines share the need to tell stories or create experiences that resonate with audiences, but the tools, workflows, and career structures of each are distinct. Most paths are portfolio-driven rather than credential-driven. Day to day, working in this field means constant iteration, tight deadlines, collaboration with other creative professionals, and the discipline to produce consistently when inspiration is not present. The distribution landscape has changed enormously — individual creators now reach audiences that previously required institutional infrastructure.
keySkills: Technical proficiency with the production tools specific to your discipline
Storytelling and narrative structure in your medium — visual, audio, or interactive
Working within production workflows, timelines, and revision processes
Collaborating with directors, clients, and creative collaborators effectively
Building a body of work that demonstrates a consistent creative voice
Understanding how your medium is distributed and what audiences respond to
opportunities: Videographer, director, or editor in commercial and narrative film
Music producer working with artists or producing library and sync music
Sound designer or audio engineer for film, games, and live events
Podcast producer at media companies or as an independent creator
Social media content creator building audiences on digital platforms
Game designer at studios of all sizes

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand how the media production landscape is structured — the roles, the workflows, and the entry points into each discipline. Pick one specialization and understand its specific tools, community, and portfolio requirements.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation and Production
journeyPhases.focus: Make work constantly. Volume of practice matters more in creative production than in most other fields. Study what makes strong work in your specific discipline through rigorous critical viewing or listening.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Build a showreel, portfolio, or published catalog of work. Apply for roles, take on collaborative projects, and enter your work into competitions or festivals relevant to your discipline.

title: Architecture and Spatial Design
summary: Design the buildings, spaces, and objects people inhabit and use every day. From permanent structures that outlast their designers to everyday objects people hold in their hands.
description: Architecture and spatial design covers the disciplines that shape the built and physical environment — architecture, interior design, and industrial and product design. Architecture is the most demanding path, requiring a protected professional qualification (typically 7–9 years total) before you can use the title independently. Interior design and product design have more accessible entry points, with portfolio routes viable alongside or instead of formal degrees. What unites these disciplines is three-dimensional spatial thinking — the ability to understand how space, light, material, and human behavior interact — and the technical skills to realize a design concept in the physical world. The field rewards people who are both visually precise and technically rigorous.
keySkills: Developing spatial concepts through sketch, model, and technical drawing
Applying material knowledge to design decisions with awareness of performance and aesthetics
Using 3D modeling and visualization tools (Rhino, SketchUp, Fusion 360, or Revit)
Understanding construction methods, structural constraints, and manufacturing processes
Presenting design work to clients and collaborators with clear visual and verbal communication
Translating human needs and behavioral patterns into physical environments or objects
opportunities: Architect in residential, commercial, or specialist practices
Interior designer in hospitality, commercial, or high-end residential settings
Industrial or product designer at consumer goods or technology companies
Set designer or production designer for film, television, or live events
Exhibition or retail designer creating branded physical environments
Urban designer working at the intersection of architecture and planning
verificationNote: The title of architect is legally protected in most countries and requires registration; qualification and registration requirements vary significantly by region.

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the significant differences in commitment level between architecture (7–9 years to full qualification), interior design (accessible via portfolio route), and product design (hybrid path). Choose your specific direction before committing to a program.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation and Training
journeyPhases.focus: Complete the relevant training for your discipline. Architecture requires a full academic program. Interior and product design can be entered through shorter courses or self-directed portfolio development alongside mentorship or studio experience.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Practice
journeyPhases.focus: Begin working in your discipline — as an architectural assistant, junior interior designer, or graduate product designer. Build a portfolio of completed projects and work toward professional qualification or registration where relevant.

title: Writing and Content
summary: Communicate with words at every scale — journalism, fiction, UX copy, and content strategy. The discipline at the center of every media product, technology interface, and cultural conversation.
description: Writing and content covers the full range of professional writing disciplines — journalism and creative writing for media and publishing, and UX writing and content design for digital products. These paths share the fundamental skill of writing clearly and purposefully, but diverge significantly in their creative context, career structure, and audience. Journalists and creative writers build public readerships and often work independently or for media organizations. UX writers and content designers are embedded in product teams, writing the functional copy inside apps and platforms. Both require genuine facility with language, an understanding of the audience you are writing for, and the discipline to produce work to brief and deadline.
keySkills: Writing clearly, precisely, and with appropriate tone for your specific audience and context
Editing your own work rigorously and responding constructively to editorial direction
Understanding the medium you are writing for — print, digital, in-product — and how it affects the work
Researching topics accurately and verifying information before publishing
Building a body of published or portfolio work that demonstrates range and consistent quality
Managing deadlines and multiple writing projects simultaneously
opportunities: Staff journalist or reporter at media organizations
Freelance feature writer contributing to publications across a specialist area
Author of fiction, non-fiction, or genre work
UX writer or content designer at technology companies
Content strategist managing editorial frameworks for brands or platforms
Screenwriter or script editor for film, television, or interactive media

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the distinction between journalism, creative writing, and UX writing — they require different skills and have entirely different career structures and income models. Identify which direction genuinely aligns with both your ability and your goals.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation and Publication
journeyPhases.focus: Write constantly and publish wherever you can. Start a blog, contribute to student media, pitch to publications above your comfort level, or build UX writing case studies by rewriting existing product copy. Published work is your primary credential.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Build a focused portfolio of your best published work or writing case studies. Apply for writing roles or pitch for commissions. Writing careers often build through freelance work before transitioning to staff roles.

title: Performing Arts
summary: Live performance, movement, and the stage. The oldest art forms and still the most immediately powerful — and careers built entirely on what you can do in front of a real audience.
description: Performing arts covers the disciplines of live performance — theatre, acting, dance, and choreography. These careers are built entirely on demonstrated skill and the ability to hold attention in real time without a screen or edit between you and your audience. The career paths are predominantly portfolio and audition-based, with formal training available through conservatoires and drama schools but not mandatory for all routes. Most performing arts careers are portfolio-based and economically challenging — consistent full-time employment purely through performance is achieved by a minority of practitioners, and most build portfolio careers combining performance with teaching, directing, and other related work. The work itself is profoundly rewarding for those genuinely committed to it.
keySkills: Technical skill in your performance discipline developed to a professional standard through consistent training
Performing with presence, vulnerability, and authenticity in front of live audiences
Taking direction and adapting your work quickly in rehearsal environments
Learning and retaining large amounts of material accurately under time pressure
Navigating the audition, casting, and professional engagement processes
Building the physical and mental resilience the performance industry demands
opportunities: Actor in professional theatre, film, television, and commercial work
Dancer in professional companies, commercial work, or educational settings
Choreographer creating work for stage, screen, and live events
Drama teacher or movement educator combining performance with teaching
Theatre director leading productions at fringe, regional, or major venues
Performance coach applying physical and vocal training to non-performance contexts

journeyPhases.name: Field Orientation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the performing arts landscape — the difference between theatre, commercial performance, and dance, and the realistic career trajectories in each. Train with practitioners who work professionally, not just those who teach.

journeyPhases.name: Training and Development
journeyPhases.focus: Train consistently and perform in every context you can access. Drama school or conservatoire training is valuable for the network and industry access it provides, not just the technique. Portfolio careers are the norm — begin building multiple related skills early.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Career Building
journeyPhases.focus: Audition continuously, take every credit-building opportunity, and build your network within the industry. The performing arts career is non-linear and requires sustained commitment over years before professional stability becomes achievable.

title: Life Sciences
summary: Study living organisms — from the genetics of a single cell to the ecology of entire ecosystems. The scientific foundation of medicine, conservation, agriculture, and biotechnology.
description: Life sciences covers the biological disciplines that study living organisms and their systems — marine biology, biotechnology, genetics and genomics, ecology, conservation biology, and microbiology and immunology. These disciplines share a common foundation in cell biology, biochemistry, and evolutionary theory, diverging into distinct specializations that range from deep-ocean research to industrial fermentation to CRISPR-based gene editing. Most careers in life sciences require at minimum a bachelor's degree; research and senior positions typically require a master's or PhD. The field attracts people who are genuinely curious about how living systems work and motivated by applications that range from treating disease to protecting endangered species.
keySkills: Applying cell biology, biochemistry, and molecular biology principles to your specialist area
Designing and conducting biological experiments with appropriate controls and statistical rigor
Working safely in laboratory or field environments with appropriate biosafety protocols
Analyzing biological data using quantitative and computational methods
Writing scientific reports, literature reviews, and research papers clearly
Understanding the connections between your specialist area and its applied implications
opportunities: Research scientist at universities, pharmaceutical companies, or research institutes
Biotechnologist at drug development or agricultural biotech companies
Conservation biologist at wildlife organizations, NGOs, or government agencies
Marine or environmental biologist conducting field research and advising policy
Clinical scientist at hospitals or diagnostic laboratories
Science communicator making biological research accessible to wider audiences

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Direction
journeyPhases.focus: Research the specific life science disciplines and identify your area of genuine interest. Understand whether your target career requires a PhD — for most research positions it does. Build strong biology and chemistry foundations before applying.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study biological sciences with increasing specialization in your chosen area. Complete a research dissertation. Develop laboratory and computational skills. Internships with pharma, biotech, or conservation organizations are highly valuable.

journeyPhases.name: Postgraduate and Entry
journeyPhases.focus: For research careers, pursue a PhD or master's degree. For applied industry roles, a master's plus relevant experience may be sufficient. Develop computational and bioinformatics skills alongside laboratory expertise.

title: Physical Sciences
summary: Understand matter, energy, and the universe at the most fundamental level. The disciplines that answer the deepest questions about reality — and produce the most mathematically transferable graduates.
description: Physical sciences covers chemistry, physics, astronomy and astrophysics, and materials science — the disciplines that study the non-living world at scales ranging from subatomic particles to galactic structures. These fields share a rigorous mathematical foundation and a commitment to understanding the fundamental laws governing physical systems. Graduates from physical sciences are among the most analytically versatile in the job market — the mathematics and problem-solving skills developed translate directly to finance, engineering, computing, and data science as well as academic and industrial research. Most research careers require a PhD; industry roles in chemistry, materials, and physics applications are accessible at undergraduate and master's level.
keySkills: Applying advanced mathematics including calculus, linear algebra, and statistics to physical problems
Designing and conducting precise experiments with rigorous uncertainty analysis
Programming in Python, MATLAB, or C++ for simulation and data analysis
Building and interpreting mathematical models of physical or chemical systems
Writing technical reports and communicating complex quantitative findings clearly
Thinking systematically about how physical systems behave and how they can be measured
opportunities: Research scientist in chemistry, physics, materials, or astronomy at universities or labs
Quantitative analyst or data scientist applying physics training to finance
Materials engineer developing new substances for aerospace, electronics, or energy
Semiconductor or photonics engineer at technology hardware companies
Chemical analyst or process chemist at pharmaceutical or industrial companies
Science teacher or communicator bringing physical sciences to broader audiences

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Direction
journeyPhases.focus: Research chemistry, physics, materials science, and astrophysics degree programs. Confirm strong mathematics and physics performance at pre-university level. Understand the applied vs. research career distinction early.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study your chosen discipline to degree level with increasing specialization. Develop programming and computational skills alongside theoretical and experimental work. Identify whether academic research or applied industry is your target.

journeyPhases.name: Specialization and Entry
journeyPhases.focus: For research careers, pursue a PhD in your specialist area. For industry and applied roles, leverage the transferability of physical science training into finance, engineering, data science, or specialist technical roles.

title: Earth and Environmental Sciences
summary: Study the planet — its history, its systems, and the forces threatening them right now. The scientific disciplines with the most direct connection to the defining challenges of the 21st century.
description: Earth and environmental sciences covers geology, environmental science, and the disciplines that study how the Earth's physical and biological systems interact and change over time. Geologists read the history of the planet in rock and sediment; environmental scientists monitor and assess the human impacts on air, water, and ecosystems; both provide essential evidence for energy, mining, infrastructure, climate science, and environmental policy. The field is increasingly data-driven, with GIS, remote sensing, and environmental modeling becoming core tools alongside traditional fieldwork. Applied careers in environmental consulting and geotechnical engineering are well-established and commercially active; research careers support the policy and science that governs environmental protection globally.
keySkills: Conducting geological or environmental field surveys and interpreting physical evidence
Using GIS and remote sensing tools for spatial analysis and mapping
Applying geochemical, hydrological, or ecological analysis to real environmental questions
Writing technical environmental or geological reports for regulatory and commercial contexts
Working effectively in field environments across varied terrain and weather conditions
Interpreting environmental data and communicating findings to non-specialist audiences
opportunities: Environmental consultant assessing environmental impacts of development projects
Geologist at engineering, mining, or oil and gas companies
Hydrogeologist managing groundwater resources or contaminated land
Environmental officer at government agencies and regulatory bodies
Climate scientist at research institutes or meteorological organizations
Geohazard specialist assessing landslide, flood, and earthquake risk

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Direction
journeyPhases.focus: Research geology, environmental science, or earth science degree programs. Understand the distinction between the environmental consulting path and the research science path — they require different specializations and lead to different career structures.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study geological or environmental science fundamentals with significant fieldwork. Develop GIS and data analysis skills. A placement year with an environmental consultancy or geological survey organization significantly improves graduate employability.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Specialization
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for graduate environmental scientist, geologist, or consultant roles. Environmental consulting provides the most accessible entry point with clear progression. Professional accreditation (FGS, CEnv) builds long-term career credibility.

title: Applied Sciences
summary: Put scientific knowledge to practical use. Forensics, food science, and agricultural science — the disciplines that keep society safe, fed, and honestly informed.
description: Applied sciences covers the scientific disciplines that directly address practical human needs — forensic science (criminal justice), food science and technology (safe and nutritious food production), and agricultural science (sustainable food systems). These fields apply the methods and knowledge of biology, chemistry, and environmental science to real-world problems with direct societal consequence. Day to day, a forensic scientist might be analyzing DNA evidence for a criminal trial; a food technologist might be developing safer preservation methods for a food manufacturer; an agronomist might be advising a farmer on disease management in their crop. All three require degree-level scientific training; postgraduate study is increasingly expected for senior and research positions.
keySkills: Applying core scientific methods (biology, chemistry, microbiology) to your specialist applied field
Working within strict quality, safety, and regulatory standards specific to your field
Designing experiments and assessments that produce evidence applicable to real decisions
Communicating scientific findings clearly in regulatory, legal, or commercial contexts
Working under conditions where accuracy is non-negotiable and errors have real consequences
Staying current with regulatory changes and scientific developments in your specific applied area
opportunities: Forensic scientist at police laboratories or private forensic providers
Food technologist at food manufacturers or regulatory agencies
Agronomist advising farmers on crop management and sustainable production
Quality assurance scientist in food, pharmaceutical, or agricultural supply chains
Regulatory affairs specialist for food, crop protection, or forensic applications
Research scientist applying agricultural or food science to sustainability challenges

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Direction
journeyPhases.focus: Research forensic science, food science, or agricultural science degree programs relevant to your target career. Understand the applied nature of these disciplines — the science serves a specific societal function, which shapes both the training and the career.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study the relevant scientific foundations with applied laboratory and fieldwork. Accreditation by relevant professional bodies is important in forensic science especially — research which programs are recognized before applying.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Specialization
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for graduate scientist roles in your target sector. Forensic science competition is high — specialist skills and postgraduate qualifications improve prospects. Food and agricultural science offer more direct entry paths with well-structured graduate programs.

title: Law and Governance
summary: The rules that hold society together — and the careers built around writing, arguing, enforcing, and reforming them. Every institution and every conflict eventually arrives at a legal or governance dimension.
description: Law and governance covers the professions and disciplines concerned with the legal and policy frameworks that organize society — lawyers and barristers who argue and advise on the law, criminologists who study crime and justice systems, urban planners who shape how cities develop, and cybersecurity policy specialists who govern how nations protect their digital infrastructure. These paths diverge enormously in training and career structure but share a common interest in how rules are made, applied, and contested. Law itself requires the longest and most structured training pathway; policy and planning roles are accessible with a broader range of degrees and backgrounds.
keySkills: Analyzing legal, regulatory, and policy frameworks with precision and critical clarity
Writing arguments, opinions, and analyses that are logically sound and legally accurate
Understanding how institutions — courts, governments, regulators — function and make decisions
Navigating competing interests and applying legal or policy frameworks to resolve them
Communicating complex legal or governance concepts clearly to non-specialist audiences
Researching legal, policy, or social science questions with rigorous methodology
opportunities: Solicitor, attorney, or barrister in private practice or public interest law
In-house counsel at corporations or government departments
Policy analyst at government ministries, think tanks, or regulatory bodies
Urban or transport planner at local authorities or consultancies
Criminologist at research institutes, probation services, or justice organizations
Cybersecurity policy advisor at government agencies or technology companies
verificationNote: Legal practice requires country-specific bar admission and registration; other law and governance roles have varying qualification and registration requirements by region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Direction
journeyPhases.focus: Understand the range from legal practice to policy, planning, and criminology — these paths share intellectual foundations but have very different working environments and training requirements. Research each direction's specific qualification pathway.

journeyPhases.name: Academic Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Complete a law or social science degree. For legal practice, qualify through the jurisdiction-specific professional training route. For policy and planning, build practical experience alongside academic credentials.

journeyPhases.name: Specialization and Entry
journeyPhases.focus: Specialize in a practice area (for law) or a policy domain (for governance roles). The first qualified position in law — training contract, pupillage, or clerkship — is the most competitive step. In policy and planning, network and work experience matter as much as qualifications.

title: Social and Behavioral Sciences
summary: Understand why people think, feel, behave, and form societies the way they do. The disciplines that explain human behavior — and are applied everywhere from clinical practice to technology design.
description: Social and behavioral sciences covers psychology, sociology, economics, social work, counseling, and anthropology — the disciplines that study individuals and societies from behavioral, structural, and cultural perspectives. These fields diverge significantly in their methods (experimental, ethnographic, quantitative) and their applications (clinical, policy, commercial, academic) but share a commitment to understanding human behavior systematically and rigorously. Graduates apply these disciplines across an enormous range of careers: clinical professionals, social researchers, policy analysts, UX researchers, organizational consultants, and public health specialists all draw on social and behavioral science foundations.
keySkills: Applying theoretical frameworks from your discipline to understand real social or behavioral phenomena
Conducting research using qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methods appropriately
Analyzing and interpreting data — statistical, observational, or narrative — with rigor
Writing analyses and reports that communicate complex social findings clearly
Working sensitively and ethically with research participants or vulnerable populations
Applying your discipline's insights to practical problems in clinical, policy, or commercial contexts
opportunities: Clinical or counseling psychologist after postgraduate training
Social worker supporting vulnerable individuals and communities
Social researcher at government agencies or policy organizations
Economic analyst at consultancies, banks, or government bodies
Anthropologist or sociologist in development, NGO, or academic roles
UX researcher applying behavioral science to digital product design

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Direction
journeyPhases.focus: Research psychology, sociology, economics, and social work as distinct disciplines with different methods, theories, and career outcomes. Identify which approach to understanding people most resonates with how you naturally think.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study your chosen discipline at degree level. Develop research methods skills — both quantitative and qualitative — as these are the most transferable capability the degree provides. Identify early whether you are targeting clinical, research, policy, or commercial careers.

journeyPhases.name: Postgraduate and Entry
journeyPhases.focus: Many applied careers in this field require postgraduate training — clinical psychology, social work, counseling, and economics research positions all typically require further study beyond the undergraduate degree.

title: International and Public Affairs
