Documenting architecture decisions and communicating tradeoffs to engineering leadership
opportunities: Cloud architect at an enterprise technology company
Solutions architect at AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure
Infrastructure architect at a financial services or insurance firm
Cloud platform architect at a healthcare or government organization
Technical architect at a cloud consulting firm
Cloud cost optimization specialist at a scale-up with growing infrastructure spend

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Build hands-on experience with one cloud provider — AWS is the best starting point. Work through core services: compute, storage, networking, IAM. Prepare for and pass the AWS Cloud Practitioner exam.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Pursue the AWS Solutions Architect Associate certification. Build real architectures using Terraform or CDK. Study failure modes and how production systems actually break at scale.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Complete a professional-level certification. Document architecture designs with decision records. Target solutions architect or senior cloud engineer roles at companies with serious cloud footprint.

title: Cybersecurity
summary: Defend systems, data, and people from threats that grow more sophisticated every year. One of the most critical and chronically understaffed technical disciplines in the world.
description: Cybersecurity professionals protect organizations from attacks on their systems, data, and people. The field is broad — it includes penetration testers who find vulnerabilities before attackers do, security engineers who build defensive systems, threat intelligence analysts who track threat actors, and GRC specialists who manage regulatory compliance. Entry into the field is possible from both self-taught certification paths and university degrees. Day to day you might be running a vulnerability scan, triaging a phishing alert, reviewing a security architecture proposal, or writing a security standard for a new engineering team. What matters most is the ability to think like an attacker.
keySkills: Identifying and exploiting common web application vulnerabilities from the OWASP Top 10
Analyzing network traffic with Wireshark to identify suspicious communication patterns
Conducting penetration tests on web apps and networks using Burp Suite and Metasploit
Implementing network security controls: firewalls, VPNs, and IDS/IPS configuration
Working with SIEM platforms like Splunk or Microsoft Sentinel to detect and investigate threats
Understanding cryptography fundamentals: symmetric encryption, TLS, hashing, and PKI
Writing security incident reports and communicating findings to technical and executive audiences
opportunities: Junior penetration tester at a cybersecurity consultancy
Security operations center (SOC) analyst at an enterprise company
Application security engineer embedded in a development team
Security engineer at a cloud-native product startup
GRC analyst at a financial services or healthcare firm
Threat intelligence analyst at a government or defense agency

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Build networking fundamentals — TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP. Learn how operating systems work at a systems level. Work toward CompTIA Security+ as your baseline credential.

journeyPhases.name: Core Skills
journeyPhases.focus: Pick a specialization: offensive (pentesting), defensive (SOC/blue team), or security engineering. Go deep in one direction. Build labs using TryHackMe, HackTheBox, or a home virtual environment.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Earn a specialist credential (CEH, eJPT, or OSCP for offensive; CySA+ for defensive). Build a portfolio of CTF write-ups or bug bounty submissions. Apply for entry-level SOC analyst or junior pentester roles.

title: Cybersecurity Analysis
summary: Investigate attacks, trace breaches, and protect infrastructure when threats get through. Equal parts detective and engineer — and one of the most direct entry paths into the cybersecurity field.
description: Cybersecurity analysts monitor, detect, investigate, and respond to security incidents inside organizations. You work in Security Operations Centers (SOCs), reviewing alerts from SIEM tools, triaging phishing reports, tracing lateral movement after a breach, and writing incident reports that explain what happened and how to prevent recurrence. Unlike penetration testers who simulate attacks, you deal with real threats in real time. You need a strong mental model of how attackers move through systems — so you can recognize patterns in alerts that would otherwise look like noise. This is the most common entry point into the broader cybersecurity field.
keySkills: Triaging and investigating security alerts in SIEM platforms like Splunk or Microsoft Sentinel
Conducting digital forensics on endpoints and network logs to reconstruct incident timelines
Analyzing malware samples in sandboxed environments to understand their behavior
Writing detailed incident reports communicating impact, timeline, and remediation steps
Using threat intelligence feeds to contextualize indicators of compromise (IOCs)
Mapping observed attacker behavior to the MITRE ATT&CK framework
Running vulnerability scans and prioritizing remediation based on business risk
opportunities: SOC analyst (Tier 1–3) at a managed security services provider
Incident response analyst at a financial services or healthcare firm
Threat intelligence analyst at an enterprise security team
Digital forensics examiner at a law enforcement agency or consultancy
Security analyst at a government cybersecurity agency
Vulnerability management analyst at a large enterprise organization

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Learn networking, operating systems, and core threat concepts. Earn CompTIA Security+ or Network+. Set up a home lab to practice log analysis and basic incident response workflows.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Get hands-on with SIEM tools. Work through TryHackMe or HackTheBox Blue Team labs. Study the MITRE ATT&CK framework and practice mapping real alerts to tactics and techniques.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Earn CompTIA CySA+ or the Blue Team Labs Level 1 credential. Write up lab investigations as portfolio pieces. Apply for Tier 1 SOC analyst roles at MSSPs as your entry point into the field.

title: IT Systems Administration
summary: Keep the technology of organizations running. IT sysadmins are the expert everyone calls when everything stops working — and the ones quietly preventing most failures before they happen.
description: IT systems administrators manage the hardware, software, networks, and user accounts that organizations depend on daily. You configure servers, manage Active Directory, maintain network infrastructure, support end users, handle backups, and ensure that everything from email to VPNs to file servers actually functions. Day to day, you might provision a laptop for a new hire, investigate why a user cannot access a shared folder, patch a server to close a security vulnerability, or set up monitoring alerts on critical infrastructure. This is one of the most reliable paths into technology — it pays steadily, is needed everywhere, and builds foundational knowledge that transfers directly into cloud, security, or DevOps specializations.
keySkills: Managing Windows Server and Active Directory environments including Group Policy configuration
Configuring and troubleshooting TCP/IP networks, DNS, DHCP, and VLANs
Administering cloud environments including Microsoft 365 and Azure AD
Setting up, maintaining, and testing backup and disaster recovery systems
Automating repetitive tasks using PowerShell or Bash scripts
Securing endpoints with patch management and endpoint detection tools
Diagnosing hardware and software issues under pressure while supporting end users
opportunities: IT administrator at a small or mid-sized business
Systems administrator at a school or university
Network administrator at a healthcare organization
IT support specialist at a government department
Junior systems engineer at a managed IT services provider
Infrastructure technician at a legal or financial services firm

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Build core IT knowledge: networking fundamentals, operating systems, and hardware basics. Work toward CompTIA A+ or Network+ as your first credential.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Learn Windows Server and Active Directory hands-on using virtual machines. Earn CompTIA Server+ or Microsoft's AZ-900 for cloud fundamentals. Practice scripting routine tasks in PowerShell.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for help desk or junior sysadmin roles — they are plentiful and the standard entry point. Document lab projects and certifications. The goal is to get into a real environment and start accumulating production experience.

title: Embedded Systems / IoT
summary: Write code that runs inside physical devices — cars, medical equipment, smart hardware. The software the world runs on invisibly, where reliability is not negotiable.
description: Embedded systems engineers write software for microcontrollers, processors, and hardware devices where compute is constrained and reliability is non-negotiable. You work in C and C++ close to the hardware — managing memory manually, writing device drivers, handling real-time operating system constraints, and debugging with oscilloscopes and logic analyzers rather than just log files. Your software might run in a pacemaker, a factory robot, a car's braking system, or a smart thermostat. Unlike web or app development, mistakes here can have physical consequences — which is why this field demands precision and carries higher barriers to entry than most software paths.
keySkills: Writing firmware in C and C++ for microcontrollers like ARM Cortex-M or ESP32
Configuring and using real-time operating systems (RTOS) like FreeRTOS in constrained environments
Interfacing with sensors and peripherals via I2C, SPI, UART, and CAN protocols
Debugging hardware and firmware issues with JTAG debuggers and logic analyzers
Managing memory manually without dynamic allocation in resource-constrained systems
Reading circuit schematics and collaborating with hardware engineers during board design
Optimizing firmware for power consumption and deterministic real-time performance
opportunities: Embedded software engineer at an automotive Tier 1 supplier
Firmware engineer at a medical device company
IoT developer at a smart home or building automation company
Embedded systems engineer at an aerospace or defense contractor
Firmware developer at a consumer electronics manufacturer
Edge computing engineer at an industrial automation company

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Learn C deeply — pointers, memory layout, bitwise operations. Get a development kit (STM32 or ESP32) and start reading sensors, blinking LEDs, and understanding how software communicates with hardware.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Learn RTOS concepts and apply FreeRTOS on a real board. Study communication protocols. Build a complete embedded project: a sensor node, a motor controller, or a data logger with real constraints.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Document hardware projects with schematics, code, and video demonstrations. Target firmware engineer roles at IoT startups, automotive suppliers, or medical device companies.

title: UI / UX Design
summary: Make digital products easier, more human, and more intuitive. Design is not decoration — it is the product. And every team that ships software eventually learns this.
description: UI/UX designers create the look, feel, and structure of digital products — the screens, interactions, and visual systems that determine whether an app feels good to use or constantly frustrating. You work through research, wireframes, prototypes, usability testing, and high-fidelity mockups in tools like Figma. On a given day, you might run a usability test to understand why users keep abandoning a checkout flow, design new onboarding screens based on the findings, and present your reasoning to the product team. This path does not require a design degree — portfolios of real work are what get people hired — but it requires both visual judgment and the ability to ground decisions in how real users actually behave.
keySkills: Designing high-fidelity screens and interactive prototypes in Figma
Conducting usability tests and extracting actionable findings from real user sessions
Building and maintaining design systems with components, tokens, and usage documentation
Applying visual design principles: hierarchy, spacing, contrast, and typography
Collaborating with engineers to understand and respect technical constraints in design decisions
Translating user research insights into specific, testable design changes
Communicating design rationale clearly to product managers, engineers, and stakeholders
opportunities: Product designer at a SaaS startup
UX designer at a consumer app company
UI designer at a digital agency serving product brands
Design system specialist at a large technology company
Freelance product designer for B2B tools and dashboards
UX designer embedded in a healthcare or fintech product team

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Learn Figma fundamentals. Understand the core design process: research, wireframe, prototype, test, iterate. Study existing products critically — why does this feel better than that? What decision caused the difference?

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Design 2–3 complete case studies from problem definition to solution. Practice user research methods. Learn to build design systems and component libraries. Seek direct feedback from working designers.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Polish case studies to show process, not just final screens. Each project should explain the problem, your research, your decisions, and the measured outcome. Apply for junior product designer or UX designer roles.

title: Product Management
summary: Decide what gets built and why. Product managers connect user needs, business goals, and engineering reality — and are responsible for whether the result actually solves the problem.
description: Product managers define the direction of software products — they work with users, business stakeholders, and engineering teams to determine what problems are worth solving, what solutions to build, and whether the result actually worked. You spend your time writing specifications, conducting user interviews, analyzing data, running prioritization sessions, and aligning engineering and design around a shared goal. Unlike engineers who build, PMs are responsible for what gets built and why. This role attracts people from technical, business, and design backgrounds — but regardless of where you start, you need to be credible with engineers and able to translate between the language of business and the language of technology.
keySkills: Writing clear, detailed product specifications that engineering teams can build from confidently
Conducting user interviews and synthesizing findings into prioritized product decisions
Using data to evaluate feature performance and inform roadmap prioritization
Facilitating sprint planning, backlog grooming, and roadmap review sessions
Communicating product strategy and tradeoffs to engineers, designers, and executives
Running structured prioritization frameworks (RICE, MoSCoW) across competing demands
Defining success metrics for product features and evaluating them after launch
opportunities: Associate product manager (APM) at a technology company
Product manager at a B2B SaaS startup
Growth PM at a consumer app platform
Technical PM bridging engineering and business at a data-heavy company
Internal tools PM at a company with large engineering operations
Product owner coordinating a cross-functional agile software team

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Learn product frameworks: discovery, prioritization, and delivery. Understand how engineers and designers work. Study real products critically — why they exist, what decisions were made, and where they failed.

journeyPhases.name: Core Skills
journeyPhases.focus: Take on a product role in whatever capacity you can — APM program, startup, internal team, or side project. Write real specs, run real user interviews, and ship real features with real teams.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Document your product work as case studies: what you shipped, the data, and what happened. Apply for APM programs at larger companies or PM roles at early-stage startups where the scope is broader.

title: AI Product Management
summary: Bring AI-powered products from idea to launch. The role requires understanding both what a language model can actually do and what users genuinely need — a combination that is rare and increasingly valuable.
description: AI product managers define, prioritize, and ship products built on top of AI systems — language models, recommendation engines, classification models, or generative tools. You need to understand the capabilities and limitations of AI well enough to scope what is actually buildable, and understand users well enough to know what is actually useful. Day to day, you might be designing evaluation criteria for a new AI feature, reviewing model outputs with the engineering team, writing a spec for a summarization workflow, or explaining to stakeholders why a feature that works 80% of the time is not ready to ship. This role differs from traditional PM because the technology is probabilistic — and managing that uncertainty is its own skill.
keySkills: Defining evaluation criteria for AI features and interpreting model output quality at scale
Writing product specs that account for model limitations, latency, and production failure modes
Working with prompt engineers and ML engineers to scope AI features accurately
Communicating probabilistic AI behavior to non-technical stakeholders and executives
Designing fallback experiences for when AI outputs are incorrect or unhelpful
Using LLM APIs to prototype and validate AI feature concepts before full engineering investment
Running user research specifically on AI features — trust, mental models, and adoption patterns
opportunities: AI product manager at an LLM-native startup
PM for AI features at a large enterprise software company
Conversational AI product lead at a customer service or support platform
AI product manager at a consumer health, education, or finance app
Technical PM at an AI infrastructure or tooling company
Product lead for AI copilots and assistants at a SaaS company

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Build practical AI fluency — not theory, but hands-on use of LLM APIs, prompt engineering, and evaluation tools. Understand what models can and cannot do before trying to ship them in a product.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Combine AI literacy with product skills. Build a prototype AI feature end-to-end. Practice writing specs for probabilistic systems and designing evaluation frameworks that can run automatically.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Document AI product case studies — what you shipped, how you evaluated quality, and what the measured outcomes were. Apply to AI-first companies or PM roles at companies actively building AI features.

title: Technical Writing
summary: Translate complexity into clarity. Technical writers make powerful tools actually usable — and every serious engineering organization eventually learns how badly it needs them.
description: Technical writers create the documentation, guides, API references, tutorials, and changelogs that let developers, users, and teams work effectively with complex technology. You work at the boundary between engineering and everyone else — which means you need to understand what engineers built well enough to explain it accurately, and understand your audience well enough to explain it usefully. Day to day, you might be writing a getting started guide for a developer API, restructuring a disorganized reference section, editing an internal runbook, or setting up a documentation site from scratch. This career rewards people who read broadly, write precisely, and are genuinely curious about how things work.
keySkills: Writing clear, structured API documentation including endpoints, parameters, and code examples
Creating step-by-step tutorials that work for both technical and non-technical audiences
Building and maintaining documentation sites using Docusaurus, MkDocs, or ReadTheDocs
Interviewing engineers and product teams to extract knowledge and turn it into usable content
Editing technical content for accuracy, clarity, and consistency of terminology
Managing documentation as code using Git and Markdown alongside software repositories
Designing information architecture for large documentation sites and developer portals
opportunities: Technical writer at a developer tools or API-first company
Documentation engineer at an open-source software organization
API writer at a cloud platform or infrastructure company
Technical content specialist at a SaaS product company
Documentation lead at a startup scaling its engineering team
Freelance technical writer for developer-facing products and platforms

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Learn to read and write basic code samples. Understand APIs and how developer documentation works. Start documenting things you already know — a tool you've set up, an API you use regularly.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Contribute to open-source documentation projects. Build a documentation site for a real or personal project. Learn documentation tooling: Docusaurus, MkDocs, or ReadTheDocs.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Publish 3–5 documentation samples covering different formats: tutorial, reference, and conceptual overview. Apply for technical writer roles at developer-focused companies.

title: QA / Test Engineering
summary: Find what breaks before users do. The discipline that separates professional software from amateur builds — and the people who do it well are invaluable to every engineering team.
description: QA and test engineers design, build, and run the systems that verify software works correctly before it reaches users. You write automated test suites, conduct manual and exploratory testing, set up CI integration that blocks broken code from deploying, and investigate bugs with enough depth to give developers useful reproduction steps. At senior levels, you design testing strategies across entire systems — deciding what to automate, what to test manually, what risk level is acceptable, and how to measure quality over time. This is a legitimate technical career that pays well, contributes directly to product quality, and provides exposure to the entire software stack.
keySkills: Writing automated end-to-end tests using Playwright or Cypress for web applications
Designing unit and integration test suites with Jest, Vitest, or pytest
Setting up CI pipelines that run test suites automatically on every pull request
Conducting structured exploratory testing sessions to find edge cases and usability issues
Writing detailed bug reports with clear reproduction steps, environment details, and evidence
Building and maintaining API test suites using Postman or REST-assured
Analyzing test coverage and identifying gaps in the overall testing strategy
opportunities: QA engineer at a product startup or scale-up
Test automation engineer at a financial services company
Software development engineer in test (SDET) at a large technology company
Manual QA specialist at a mobile app company
Performance test engineer at a high-traffic web platform
QA lead setting testing strategy across multiple engineering teams

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Learn software testing fundamentals — types of tests, test case design, and how bug tracking workflows function. Learn basic JavaScript or Python to write your first automated tests.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Build a test suite for a real web application using Playwright or Cypress. Set it up to run in CI. Practice exploratory testing sessions and writing high-quality, reproducible bug reports.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Publish automated test suites on GitHub. Contribute test coverage to an open-source project. Apply for QA engineer or test automation engineer roles at teams that take software quality seriously.

title: Game Development
summary: Write the code behind the worlds people choose to spend hours inside. Game development is one of the most technically demanding forms of software engineering — and one of the most creatively satisfying.
description: Game developers write the code that powers interactive entertainment — physics engines, AI systems, real-time graphics rendering, multiplayer networking, and gameplay logic. You work in engines like Unity (C#) or Unreal Engine (C++) and build systems that need to run at 60+ frames per second with no perceivable lag. This is not making art or design decisions — that is the job of game designers and artists. Game developers solve hard engineering problems: how do you simulate realistic physics with minimal performance cost, or synchronize game state across 100 simultaneous players? The engineering skills transfer broadly to any real-time interactive software, including robotics, simulation, and XR.
keySkills: Building gameplay systems and mechanics in Unity with C# or Unreal Engine with C++
Implementing real-time physics and collision detection within a game engine
Developing multiplayer networking with client-server synchronization and lag compensation
Profiling and optimizing game performance to maintain stable frame rates under load
Writing game AI systems using behavior trees, state machines, and pathfinding algorithms
Integrating audio, animation state machines, and particle systems into interactive gameplay
Using version control workflows designed for large binary asset repositories (Git LFS, Perforce)
opportunities: Junior gameplay programmer at an indie or mid-size game studio
Engine or tools programmer at a AAA game company
Multiplayer systems developer at an online gaming platform
Technical game designer combining code and systems design at a small studio
VR/AR game developer building immersive interactive experiences
Game tools engineer building internal pipeline tools for art and content teams

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Choose Unity or Unreal and learn the engine basics: scenes, objects, scripting, and the game loop. Build small, complete games — not concepts. Completion matters more than quality at this stage.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Build more complex systems: AI behaviors, physics interactions, multiplayer basics, or graphics shaders depending on your focus. Complete and publish a game on itch.io or a similar platform.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Build a demo reel or portfolio of shipped games and technical experiments. Target junior programmer roles at small studios or contribute to game jams to build relationships inside the industry.

title: Robotics Engineering
summary: Build machines that sense, move, and act in the physical world. Robotics engineers are defining what the next industrial economy looks like — and the field is accelerating faster than at any point in its history.
description: Robotics engineers design and program machines that interact with physical environments — industrial robots, autonomous vehicles, surgical systems, delivery drones, and humanoid robots. You work at the intersection of mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, and software — writing control systems, implementing sensor fusion algorithms, and building the perception and planning systems that let machines understand and navigate space. You typically use ROS, C++, and Python. This is a degree-intensive field: most entry-level positions require at least a bachelor's in engineering, computer science, or a closely related discipline. The mathematical foundations — linear algebra, kinematics, control theory — are not optional.
keySkills: Building and integrating robot systems using the Robot Operating System (ROS 2)
Implementing motion planning algorithms for robot navigation in dynamic environments
Applying sensor fusion techniques to combine data from LiDAR, cameras, and IMUs
Writing real-time control loops in C++ for precise actuator control
Simulating robotic systems in Gazebo or Isaac Sim before physical hardware testing
Applying computer vision for object detection, pose estimation, and SLAM
Testing and validating robot behavior in edge cases and physical failure scenarios
opportunities: Robotics software engineer at an industrial automation company
Autonomous systems engineer at a self-driving vehicle startup
Control systems engineer at a warehouse and logistics robotics company
Surgical robotics engineer at a medical device manufacturer
Research engineer at a university robotics lab
Embedded engineer specializing in robot hardware integration and firmware

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Confirm your mathematics background — linear algebra and calculus are mandatory. Research engineering programs with robotics or mechatronics specializations. Start learning Python and C++ during the application period.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Cover core disciplines: control theory, kinematics, electronics, and programming. Work on robotics lab projects, join a competition team like RoboCup or FIRST, and secure internships at robotics companies.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Build a portfolio of robotics projects combining hardware and software. Target graduate engineer roles at industrial automation or autonomous vehicle companies, or apply for research positions.

title: Drone and UAV Technology
summary: Design, operate, or program unmanned systems used in delivery, agriculture, emergency response, and surveillance. A field growing faster than the regulatory frameworks trying to govern it.
description: Drone and UAV professionals work across a wide range of roles: pilots who operate UAVs commercially for aerial survey or emergency response, engineers who design and program flight control systems and autopilot software, and specialists who build the data processing pipelines that make drone-captured imagery useful. You might work for an agricultural company analyzing crop health via multispectral imagery, a logistics company building last-mile delivery systems, a construction firm using drones for site mapping, or a defense contractor building autonomous surveillance platforms. Commercial drone operation requires licensing in most countries, and regulations change constantly.
keySkills: Operating commercial UAV platforms and planning safe, legally compliant flight missions
Processing drone-captured imagery and LiDAR data for surveying and photogrammetry
Programming flight controllers and autopilot systems using ArduPilot or PX4
Using GIS software to analyze and present geospatial data collected from UAV surveys
Understanding and complying with airspace regulations in your specific operating region
Integrating payload systems (cameras, multispectral sensors, delivery mechanisms) into UAV platforms
Performing pre-flight inspections, post-flight maintenance, and incident documentation
opportunities: Commercial drone pilot at a surveying or mapping company
UAV engineer at a logistics or delivery technology startup
Aerial inspection specialist at an infrastructure or utilities company
Drone operator for film and media production
Agricultural drone technician at a precision farming company
UAV systems engineer at an aerospace or defense organization
verificationNote: Commercial drone operation requires government-issued certification in most countries; regulations and licensing requirements vary significantly by region and are subject to frequent change.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Obtain your commercial drone pilot license for your country. Learn airspace rules, safety protocols, and how to plan legally compliant flight missions. Understand the main UAV platforms and their payloads.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Specialize in one application area: surveying and mapping, agriculture, inspection, or engineering. Learn the relevant software — photogrammetry tools like Pix4D or DJI Terra. Build a portfolio of real missions with documented data outputs.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Document completed missions with data outputs and analysis. Target companies actively using UAVs: surveying firms, infrastructure companies, precision agriculture startups, and media production companies.

title: Mental Health Technology
summary: Build the apps and platforms that scale access to mental health support. Technology and empathy working together — one of the most purposeful directions in software in 2026.
description: Mental health technology professionals build digital products that support psychological well-being — therapy platforms, mood tracking apps, crisis intervention tools, AI-powered mental health assistants, and digital therapeutics. You need strong product and engineering skills combined with a genuine understanding of the clinical, ethical, and regulatory dimensions of health technology. Day to day, you might be building a session scheduling system for a teletherapy platform, integrating an AI screening tool for a healthcare provider, or ensuring a mental health app meets HIPAA compliance. The field requires sensitivity about what technology can and cannot responsibly do — a product that overpromises can cause real harm to vulnerable people.
keySkills: Building web and mobile applications compliant with HIPAA and health data privacy regulations
Integrating telehealth video infrastructure and encrypted messaging systems securely
Designing user flows that account for users who may be in distress or emotional crisis
Implementing AI features for psychoeducation, screening, and triage responsibly
Working with clinical stakeholders to validate that digital tools meet therapeutic standards
Applying trauma-informed and accessibility principles to every stage of product design
Understanding the regulatory landscape for digital health applications and clinical software
opportunities: Software engineer at a teletherapy platform
Product manager for a digital mental health application
Health tech engineer at a crisis intervention organization
Developer building clinical decision support tools for psychiatric care teams
AI product specialist at a mental health and wellness startup
Digital health engineer at a health insurance company's digital product division

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Build technical skills in web or mobile development. Study mental health basics — how therapy works, what crisis response looks like, and what HIPAA means for digital products in practice.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Build a health-adjacent product or feature that operates within clinical and privacy constraints. Understand the ethical considerations that make mental health tech fundamentally different from other consumer apps.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Target roles at established teletherapy platforms, digital therapeutics companies, or mental health non-profits building technology. Your understanding of the user population is as important as your technical skills.

title: Fintech Development
summary: Build the next generation of banking, payments, and financial tools. Where software engineering meets the movement of money — with all the compliance, correctness, and security that demands.
description: Fintech developers build the technical infrastructure behind digital banking, payments, lending, trading, and financial data products. You work on systems where correctness is not optional — a rounding error in payment processing or a race condition in a transaction system can cause real financial harm at scale. You will integrate with banking APIs, payment rails, and work under regulatory frameworks that govern how data is stored and how money moves. Day to day, you might be building a KYC onboarding flow, debugging a failed transaction, integrating an open banking API, or implementing PCI-DSS-compliant card handling. This path rewards engineers who are methodical, security-conscious, and comfortable operating in complex domain environments.
keySkills: Building payment integration flows with Stripe, Adyen, or core banking APIs
Implementing KYC and AML verification flows with third-party identity providers
Designing transaction ledger systems that are correct, auditable, and race-condition-safe
Writing idempotent API handlers for financial operations that cannot safely run twice
Implementing security controls required for PCI-DSS compliance in cardholder data environments
Working with financial data formats and standards including ISO 20022
Building reconciliation systems that detect and resolve discrepancies in financial data
opportunities: Backend engineer at a digital bank or neobank
Payments engineer at an e-commerce or marketplace platform
API developer at a financial data aggregation company
Core banking developer at a financial software vendor
Blockchain engineer at a crypto financial infrastructure company
Software engineer at a lending or credit technology startup

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Build strong backend fundamentals — APIs, databases, authentication. Learn how the financial system works: how payments move, what a ledger is, how banks communicate via APIs and messaging standards.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Build a real payments integration using Stripe or similar. Study financial API design patterns — idempotency, webhook handling, reconciliation. Learn the compliance requirements that constrain what you can build.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Build a portfolio project that handles money responsibly — a payment flow, a simple ledger, or a financial data aggregation tool. Apply for backend or platform engineer roles at fintechs, neobanks, or payments companies.

title: Medicine (General Practice)
summary: Be the first person someone trusts when something is wrong with their health. General practice is the most human-facing role in medicine — long-term patient relationships and the weight of real diagnostic responsibility every day.
description: General practitioners diagnose and treat a wide range of conditions, coordinate specialist care, and maintain ongoing relationships with patients across years. Your day includes consultations that range from a child's ear infection to an unexplained weight loss that turns out to be something serious. You need to be a generalist who makes good decisions under uncertainty, communicates complex information to frightened people, and recognizes when something requires urgent escalation. This is one of the longest educational paths in any field — medical school followed by residency and specialty training — but it is also one of the most secure, meaningful, and deeply human careers in existence.
keySkills: Conducting structured patient consultations and taking comprehensive medical histories
Performing physical examinations and interpreting diagnostic test results
Diagnosing and managing common acute and chronic conditions across all body systems
Prescribing medications appropriately and monitoring for adverse effects and interactions
Recognizing red flag symptoms that require urgent specialist referral
Communicating diagnoses, prognoses, and treatment plans clearly to patients and families
Maintaining accurate medical records and navigating electronic health record systems
opportunities: GP partner or salaried GP at a family practice
Hospital-based general medicine physician
Rural or remote area doctor providing comprehensive primary care
Medical officer at a community health center or public health clinic
Occupational physician providing workplace health services for organizations
GP academic combining clinical practice with medical education or research
verificationNote: Medical practice requires country-specific licensing and board examinations; requirements for medical school entry, residency, and registration vary significantly by region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research medical school entry requirements for your country — they vary enormously. Prepare for entrance exams (MCAT, UCAT, or equivalent). Get clinical exposure through shadowing or volunteering to confirm it is genuinely the right path before committing.

journeyPhases.name: Medical School
journeyPhases.focus: Study anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, and clinical medicine. Clinical rotations expose you to every major specialty. Pass your licensing examinations and graduate with your medical degree.

journeyPhases.name: Residency and GP Training
journeyPhases.focus: Complete foundation training and then GP specialty training in supervised clinical settings. Real clinical judgment develops here. Full registration and independent practice rights come at the completion of this phase.

title: Pharmacy
summary: Be the expert on what goes into the body and why. Pharmacists are the medication safety specialists at the intersection of clinical knowledge, chemistry, and direct patient care.
description: Pharmacists are the professionals responsible for ensuring patients receive the right medication at the right dose with the right counseling about how to use it. You work in hospitals, community pharmacies, clinical settings, research, and industry. Day to day, you might review prescriptions for interactions, counsel a patient about a new medication regimen, advise a physician on optimal dosing, or manage the medication supply chain for a ward. This is a degree-regulated profession in every country — pharmacists require a pharmacy degree plus supervised practice and registration to dispense. It is one of the most consistently in-demand healthcare roles globally.
keySkills: Reviewing prescriptions for accuracy, appropriateness, and drug interaction risks
Counseling patients on medication use, side effects, and adherence strategies
Calculating precise dosing for intravenous medications and special populations
Applying pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics principles to patient cases
Managing pharmaceutical inventory, controlled substance regulations, and dispensing records
Collaborating with physicians and clinical teams on medication therapy management
Staying current with drug approvals, safety alerts, and evidence-based prescribing guidelines
opportunities: Community pharmacist at an independent or chain pharmacy
Clinical pharmacist in a hospital ward or critical care unit
Pharmaceutical industry pharmacist in regulatory affairs or drug safety
Research pharmacist at a clinical trials organization
Pharmacy manager at a healthcare system or hospital network
Specialist pharmacist in oncology, pediatrics, or mental health settings
verificationNote: Pharmacy practice requires country-specific licensing and registration; board examination requirements and supervised practice hours vary by region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Confirm chemistry and biology foundations meet entry requirements. Research pharmacy school programs in your country. Get pharmacy volunteer or shadowing experience to understand the day-to-day role before applying.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study pharmaceutical sciences, clinical pharmacology, and pharmacy practice. Complete supervised clinical placements in community and hospital settings. Pass licensing examinations required for registration.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Complete supervised pre-registration practice required for licensure. Specialization in clinical, industrial, or community pharmacy typically begins here. Registration grants full independent practice rights.

title: Dentistry
summary: Give people something they use every day without thinking about: a healthy, functioning, confident smile. Dentistry combines clinical precision with genuine patient relationships.
description: Dentists diagnose and treat conditions affecting teeth, gums, and oral structures — and contribute significantly to overall systemic health. Day to day, you might perform fillings, extractions, root canals, cosmetic procedures, or identify early signs of oral cancer during a routine examination. Dentistry requires both fine motor precision and the interpersonal skill to work with patients who are often anxious. You will run a significant amount of your career as a small business owner in private practice, which means business and management decisions come with the clinical ones. This is one of the most autonomous healthcare careers — a practice owner makes clinical and commercial decisions independently.
keySkills: Performing examinations, diagnoses, and treatment planning for dental conditions
Executing restorative procedures including fillings, crowns, and root canal therapy
Administering local anesthesia safely and managing patient anxiety during procedures
Interpreting dental radiographs for early detection of decay and bone loss
Performing extractions, minor oral surgery, and post-operative care management
Communicating treatment plans, costs, and options clearly to patients and families
Managing a dental practice including staff, scheduling, and regulatory compliance
opportunities: Associate dentist at an established private dental practice
NHS or public health dentist providing primary care to the general population
Dental practice owner operating an independent or group practice
Specialist dentist in orthodontics, oral surgery, or periodontology after further training
Academic dentist combining clinical practice with university teaching and research
Military or humanitarian dentist providing care in specialized settings
verificationNote: Dental practice requires country-specific licensing and registration; dental board examinations and clinical competency assessments vary significantly by region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Confirm entry requirements for dental programs in your country. Prepare for admissions tests (UCAT or DAT where applicable). Get work experience in a dental setting to confirm the clinical environment suits you.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study dental sciences and clinical techniques. Treat real patients under supervision in a dental school clinic. Pass national or regional licensing examinations. Graduate with a dental degree recognized for registration.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Complete a supervised foundation year (required in many countries). Begin associate practice at an established clinic. Consider early specialist training applications if pursuing orthodontics, oral surgery, or other specialties.

title: Optometry
summary: Protect and restore the sense people rely on most. The difference between struggling and seeing clearly — every single day, for every patient you see.
description: Optometrists examine eyes, diagnose visual conditions and eye diseases, prescribe corrective lenses, and provide primary eye care. You test visual acuity, assess eye muscle function, check for glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, and other conditions, and prescribe glasses or contact lenses. You are often the first clinician to detect systemic diseases like diabetes or hypertension through changes in the eye. Most optometrists work in private practice or retail optical settings with significant clinical autonomy. This is a degree-regulated profession requiring licensure in every country, and the demand is consistent because vision problems affect most of the global population.
keySkills: Conducting comprehensive eye examinations including refraction and binocular vision assessment
Diagnosing and managing common eye conditions including dry eye, glaucoma, and macular degeneration
Prescribing and fitting corrective lenses including spectacles and contact lenses
Using slit lamp biomicroscopy and retinal imaging equipment for clinical assessment
Detecting systemic disease signs in fundus examination and referring appropriately
Managing patient records and communicating examination findings clearly
Running a clinical practice including scheduling, patient management, and regulatory compliance
opportunities: Community optometrist at an independent or retail optical practice
Hospital optometrist in a ophthalmology or low vision department
Academic optometrist combining clinical practice with research and teaching
Corporate optometrist in large retail optical chains
Specialist optometrist in contact lens practice or pediatric optometry
Optometrist in a humanitarian or remote healthcare setting
verificationNote: Optometry practice requires country-specific licensing and registration; scope of practice and examination requirements vary significantly by region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research optometry degree programs and entry requirements in your country. Get work experience shadowing a practicing optometrist. Confirm the clinical and patient-facing nature of the role is well-suited to you.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study ocular anatomy, visual optics, contact lens practice, and clinical optometry. Treat patients under supervision in a clinical setting. Pass board examinations required for registration in your country.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Complete pre-registration supervised practice (required in most countries). Begin independent practice after registration. Consider specialization in areas like pediatric optometry or low vision rehabilitation.

title: Veterinary Medicine
summary: Care for animals that cannot tell you where it hurts. Veterinary medicine demands diagnostic skill and genuine compassion in equal measure — and the work spans companion animals, wildlife, and entire food systems.
description: Veterinarians diagnose, treat, and prevent disease across a vast range of species — companion animals in private practice, livestock on farms, wildlife in conservation settings, and laboratory animals in research. You perform surgery, interpret diagnostic imaging, prescribe medications, carry out post-mortem examinations, and advise owners on preventive care. Veterinary medicine is one of the most scientifically rigorous training pathways in healthcare, with entry requirements at least as demanding as human medicine. The field is broader than most people realize: many vets work in public health, food safety, pharmaceutical development, or global disease surveillance rather than clinical practice.
keySkills: Conducting thorough clinical examinations across multiple species with different normal ranges
Performing and interpreting diagnostic tests including blood work, imaging, and microbiology
Executing surgical procedures from routine neutering to emergency trauma surgery
Prescribing and compounding medications appropriate for species-specific pharmacology
Communicating diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment options to animal owners under emotional pressure
Managing zoonotic disease risks and advising on animal biosecurity and herd health
Applying wildlife or production animal health knowledge in field settings beyond the clinic
opportunities: Companion animal vet at a private veterinary practice
Emergency vet at a specialist animal hospital
Large animal vet providing farm and agricultural veterinary services
Government veterinary officer in food safety or animal disease surveillance
Research veterinarian at a pharmaceutical company or university
Zoo or wildlife vet working with conservation programs
verificationNote: Veterinary practice requires country-specific licensing and registration with the national veterinary council or regulatory body; requirements vary by region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Accumulate required animal handling and veterinary work experience hours — most programs demand this before application. Confirm science grades meet entry requirements. Research school programs and their species focus areas.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study veterinary anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology, and clinical medicine. Rotate through clinical specialties in final years. Pass licensing examinations required for registration.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Begin work as a new graduate vet under experienced mentors. Develop clinical confidence across common presentations. Consider a residency or internship if pursuing specialist certification.

title: Emergency Medicine / Paramedicine
summary: Treat people in the worst moments of their lives — fast, in unpredictable conditions, when every minute matters. High-stakes, deeply meaningful, and unlike any other healthcare role.
description: Emergency medicine and paramedicine professionals respond to acute illness and injury in the most time-critical clinical situations. Paramedics operate in the pre-hospital environment — ambulances, air rescue, and emergency scenes — providing life-saving interventions before patients reach a hospital. Emergency physicians work in hospital emergency departments, managing the full spectrum of critical presentations from cardiac arrest to poisoning to traumatic injury. Both roles demand rapid clinical decision-making, procedural skills under pressure, and the ability to work effectively in chaotic environments. Paramedic training is typically a vocational or degree program with strict clinical placement requirements.
keySkills: Performing rapid patient assessment and clinical decision-making under time pressure
Executing life-saving interventions: airway management, IV access, defibrillation, and drug administration
Recognizing and managing major trauma, cardiac emergencies, stroke, and respiratory failure
Operating and maintaining emergency medical equipment including monitoring and airway devices
Communicating effectively with patients, families, and hospital receiving teams under stress
Documenting clinical interventions accurately in pre-hospital or emergency department records
Working as part of a multi-disciplinary emergency team with clear handover communication
opportunities: Paramedic with a national or regional ambulance service
Critical care paramedic or flight medic in helicopter emergency medical services
Emergency physician in a hospital emergency department after medical school and residency
Emergency department nurse practitioner after advanced nursing training
Wilderness medicine practitioner in remote or expedition settings
Disaster response medic with a humanitarian organization or military
verificationNote: Emergency medical and paramedic certification requirements vary by country; clinical placement hours, scope of practice, and registration are all regulated differently by region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research paramedicine programs in your country — degree and diploma routes both exist. Confirm physical fitness requirements and any prerequisite first aid certifications. Understand the scope of practice in your region before committing.

journeyPhases.name: Degree or Diploma Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, and emergency clinical skills. Complete supervised clinical placements on ambulances and in hospital emergency departments. Pass certification examinations required for licensure.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Begin supervised practice as a newly registered paramedic. Accumulate diverse case experience across medical and trauma presentations. Consider specialist training in critical care or flight paramedicine after foundational experience.

title: Midwifery
summary: Guide and protect one of the most significant experiences in a person's life. Midwifery sits at the intersection of clinical expertise and profound human trust.
description: Midwives provide care to pregnant people, those giving birth, and new parents in the postnatal period. You monitor maternal and fetal wellbeing throughout pregnancy, support physiological birth, manage complications and emergencies, and provide postnatal care to mothers and newborns. Midwives hold significant clinical autonomy — in many countries, they manage low-risk pregnancies and births independently without physician involvement. This is a registered profession requiring a degree and national registration in every country. The role requires both advanced clinical skill and exceptional interpersonal sensitivity — you are present for one of the most vulnerable and significant events in any person's life.
keySkills: Conducting antenatal assessments including fetal monitoring and risk screening
Supporting physiological labor and birth and recognizing when to escalate to obstetric care
Managing obstetric emergencies including postpartum hemorrhage and shoulder dystocia
Providing postnatal care for mothers and newborns including breastfeeding support
Administering medications including oxytocin, analgesia, and neonatal resuscitation drugs
Communicating clearly with families through complex decisions during labor and birth
Documenting clinical care and maintaining accurate maternity records
opportunities: Community midwife supporting home and birth center deliveries
Hospital midwife in a labor ward, postnatal ward, or antenatal clinic
Independent midwife providing continuity of care in private practice
Neonatal specialist midwife in a neonatal intensive care unit
Midwifery lecturer or academic in a university program
International development midwife with a humanitarian or global health organization
verificationNote: Midwifery practice requires national registration and licensing; scope of practice, supervised hours, and registration requirements vary significantly by country.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research midwifery degree programs in your country. Gain experience in a maternity or healthcare setting. Confirm your understanding of the physical and emotional demands of the role before applying.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study anatomy, physiology of pregnancy and birth, pharmacology, and midwifery practice. Complete clinical placements across community and hospital settings. Pass registration examinations.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Begin practice as a newly registered midwife under experienced mentorship. Build clinical confidence across the full maternity care pathway. Consider advanced practice or community midwifery specialization.

title: Nursing
summary: Be the most constant presence in a patient's care. Clinical skill, genuine emotional intelligence, and real human connection — every single shift, across every setting in healthcare.
description: Registered nurses are the clinical backbone of healthcare systems — they assess patients, administer medications, perform clinical procedures, monitor for deterioration, and coordinate care across multidisciplinary teams. You work in hospitals, community clinics, schools, aged care facilities, operating theaters, and people's homes. Unlike many healthcare roles, nurses work across every specialty — from emergency departments to neonatal intensive care to mental health to oncology. Nursing requires both technical precision and the emotional capacity to support people through fear, pain, and loss. It is one of the most in-demand professions globally and one of the most reliably employed.
keySkills: Conducting patient assessments and interpreting vital signs for clinical deterioration
Administering medications safely including IV, oral, and subcutaneous routes
Performing clinical procedures: wound care, catheterization, cannulation, and NG tube insertion
Recognizing and escalating acute deterioration using early warning score systems
Communicating effectively with patients, families, and multidisciplinary team members
Documenting patient care accurately and maintaining confidentiality in clinical records
Providing emotional support to patients and families during difficult and frightening situations
opportunities: Staff nurse in a hospital medical or surgical ward
Emergency department nurse in a major trauma center
ICU or critical care nurse in a specialist intensive care unit
Community nurse providing home-based clinical care
Pediatric nurse in a children's hospital or neonatal unit
Practice nurse at a GP surgery or primary care clinic
verificationNote: Nursing registration requirements vary by country; clinical placement hours, licensing examinations, and scope of practice are all regulated differently by national nursing councils.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research nursing degree programs and entry requirements in your country. Get healthcare work or volunteering experience to confirm the clinical environment is genuinely right for you before committing.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, and nursing practice. Alternate between academic study and supervised clinical placements across different healthcare settings. Pass registration assessments.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Begin work as a newly qualified nurse with a structured preceptorship program. Develop clinical confidence and speed. Consider specialist areas — emergency, critical care, oncology, or community — based on experience.

title: Physiotherapy
summary: Help people move again after injury, illness, or surgery. Recovery is deeply personal — and physiotherapists are at the center of it.
description: Physiotherapists assess and treat physical conditions that affect movement, function, and quality of life — helping people recover from sports injuries, strokes, surgery, chronic pain, and respiratory conditions. You design and deliver rehabilitation programs, apply manual therapy, teach exercise, and use electrophysical modalities to reduce pain and restore function. Day to day, you might work with a post-operative knee replacement patient, manage a chronic low back pain program, or treat a stroke survivor relearning to walk. Physiotherapy requires strong anatomical knowledge, excellent communication skills, and the patience to work with patients over weeks or months as progress is gradual.
keySkills: Conducting comprehensive musculoskeletal and neurological physiotherapy assessments
Designing evidence-based rehabilitation programs tailored to individual patient goals
Applying manual therapy techniques including joint mobilization and soft tissue treatment
Prescribing and progressing therapeutic exercise for rehabilitation and injury prevention
Treating respiratory conditions using airway clearance and breathing exercise techniques
Educating patients about pain science, movement, and self-management strategies
Documenting clinical outcomes and adjusting treatment plans based on patient progress
opportunities: Musculoskeletal physiotherapist at a private clinic or sports injury center
Hospital physiotherapist in an orthopedic, respiratory, or neurology ward
Sports physiotherapist working with elite or community sports teams
Pediatric physiotherapist in a children's hospital or community setting
Neurological physiotherapist specializing in stroke and brain injury rehabilitation
Physiotherapy practice owner running an independent clinical business
verificationNote: Physiotherapy licensing and registration requirements vary by country; some regions require additional board examinations for full independent practice rights.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research physiotherapy degree programs in your country. Get observation hours with practicing physiotherapists — required by most programs and essential for confirming fit. Ensure science prerequisites are met.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study anatomy, physiology, pathology, and physiotherapy practice across musculoskeletal, neurological, and respiratory specialties. Complete clinical placements in hospital and community settings.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Begin work as a newly graduated physiotherapist with structured supervision. Develop clinical confidence across common presentations. Consider postgraduate specialization in sports, pediatrics, or neurology.

title: Occupational Therapy
summary: Help people reclaim independence in daily life after illness, injury, or disability. Practical, compassionate, and genuinely life-changing work.
description: Occupational therapists help people regain the ability to perform daily activities — washing, dressing, cooking, working, and engaging in the activities that give their life meaning — after they have been disrupted by illness, accident, stroke, developmental conditions, or mental health. You assess functional limitations, adapt environments, prescribe assistive equipment, and design activity-based interventions that rebuild capacity and confidence. OTs work in hospitals, rehabilitation centers, community settings, schools, workplaces, and mental health services. This is one of the most person-centered roles in all of healthcare — the measure of success is not just clinical improvement but whether a person can live the life they want.
keySkills: Conducting functional assessments to identify barriers to daily living activities
Designing therapeutic activity programs to rebuild physical and cognitive function
Prescribing and training patients in the use of adaptive equipment and assistive technology
Assessing and modifying home environments to support safe independent living
Working with patients with neurological, physical, and mental health conditions across the lifespan
Documenting goal-based treatment plans and measuring functional outcomes
Collaborating with multidisciplinary teams including physio, nursing, and social work
opportunities: Community occupational therapist supporting home-based rehabilitation
Hospital OT in an acute inpatient or rehabilitation ward
Pediatric OT in a school, early intervention, or children's hospital setting
Mental health OT in an inpatient or community mental health service
Vocational rehabilitation OT supporting return to work after illness
Assistive technology OT specializing in equipment and home modification assessment
verificationNote: Occupational therapy licensing and registration requirements vary by country; check local regulatory body requirements before applying to programs.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research OT programs and entry requirements. Complete observation hours in clinical OT settings — required by most programs. Understand the breadth of the role across physical, mental health, and community settings.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study occupational science, anatomy, psychology, and OT practice. Complete supervised placements across physical rehabilitation, mental health, and community settings. Pass registration assessments.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Begin practice with structured supervision as a newly registered OT. Develop clinical reasoning and caseload management skills. Identify your preferred specialty area for further professional development.

title: Radiography / Medical Imaging
summary: See inside the body without opening it. Your images guide diagnoses and surgical decisions across every hospital, every day — work that is invisible until it is urgently needed.
description: Radiographers produce the medical images that clinicians use to diagnose disease, plan treatment, and guide procedures. You operate X-ray machines, CT and MRI scanners, ultrasound equipment, and fluoroscopy systems to capture precise images of anatomy and pathology. Beyond operating equipment, you position patients accurately, minimize radiation dose, and assess image quality to ensure clinical utility. In interventional radiography, you work alongside physicians to guide catheters, biopsies, and minimally invasive procedures in real time using live imaging. This is a technically precise role that combines equipment expertise with patient care — most patients you see are unwell, anxious, or in pain.
keySkills: Positioning patients accurately for diagnostic X-ray, CT, and MRI examinations
Operating and optimizing CT, MRI, and X-ray equipment for different clinical indications
Minimizing radiation dose while maintaining diagnostic image quality using ALARA principles
Assessing image quality and identifying technical or clinical findings requiring review
Managing patient communication and care during imaging in patients who may be unwell
Administering contrast media and monitoring patients for adverse reactions
Working safely in radiation environments and applying radiation protection procedures
opportunities: Diagnostic radiographer in a hospital imaging department
MRI or CT radiographer in a specialist imaging center
Interventional radiographer assisting image-guided clinical procedures
Nuclear medicine technologist in an isotope imaging department
Radiography educator or clinical educator in a university training program
Medical imaging manager overseeing a hospital imaging department
verificationNote: Radiography practice requires country-specific registration; licensing, radiation licensing, and scope of practice vary significantly by region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research radiography degree programs and entry requirements. Get observation hours in a hospital imaging department if possible. Confirm science prerequisites — physics and biology are central to the curriculum.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study anatomy, radiation physics, imaging technology, and clinical practice. Complete supervised clinical placements across X-ray, CT, MRI, and other modalities. Pass registration assessments.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Begin work as a registered radiographer with a supervised competency program. Develop speed and clinical judgment across common and complex examinations. Consider CT, MRI, or interventional specialization.

title: Nutrition and Dietetics
summary: Translate the science of food into personal guidance that changes how people feel and live. A field growing rapidly as the link between diet and health becomes impossible to ignore.
description: Dietitians apply the evidence-based science of nutrition to prevent and treat disease, optimize health, and support people through major illness. You might manage therapeutic nutrition for a patient on dialysis, design a weight management program for someone with type 2 diabetes, support cancer patients maintaining nutrition through chemotherapy, or advise parents on early childhood feeding. Unlike nutritionists (an unregulated title in many countries), registered dietitians are clinically trained and legally recognized healthcare professionals. You work in hospitals, community health, public health agencies, sport, private practice, and the food industry. The field sits at the intersection of biochemistry, clinical medicine, and behavioral science.
keySkills: Conducting detailed dietary assessments and nutritional screenings across clinical populations
Designing individualized therapeutic nutrition plans for conditions like diabetes, renal disease, and eating disorders
Calculating enteral and parenteral nutrition requirements for critically ill or non-oral patients
Translating complex nutritional science into practical, culturally appropriate dietary advice
Interpreting biochemical markers and anthropometric data to assess nutritional status
Delivering nutrition education and behavior change support at individual and group level
Critically appraising nutrition research to apply evidence to clinical practice
opportunities: Clinical dietitian in a hospital ward (renal, oncology, gastroenterology, or ICU)
Community dietitian providing dietary counseling in primary care or public health
Sports dietitian working with elite or recreational athletes and sports organizations
Private practice dietitian specializing in weight management or gut health
Food industry dietitian in product development, labeling, or corporate nutrition
Public health nutritionist designing population-level food and nutrition policy
verificationNote: Dietitian registration and licensing vary by country; clinical placement requirements and registration examinations differ by region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research dietetics degree programs accredited in your country. Ensure chemistry and biology prerequisites are met. Understand the distinction between a registered dietitian and an unregulated nutritionist in your region.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study biochemistry, physiology, nutrition science, food science, and clinical dietetics. Complete supervised clinical placements across hospital and community settings. Pass registration examinations.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Begin as a junior dietitian in a hospital or community setting with structured supervision. Develop caseload management and clinical reasoning skills. Identify specialist areas for further training.

title: Speech-Language Pathology
summary: Help people communicate and swallow again after stroke, injury, or developmental difficulty. A career that restores one of the most fundamental human connections — the ability to be understood.
description: Speech-language pathologists (also called speech therapists) assess and treat disorders of speech, language, communication, and swallowing. You might work with a child with autism developing language skills, an adult recovering language after a stroke, a teenager who stutters, a Parkinson's patient managing dysphagia, or a person who has lost their voice to laryngeal cancer. You design and deliver therapy, provide family education, and work closely with neurologists, pediatricians, teachers, and other healthcare professionals. This is a graduate-level profession with highly varied and deeply meaningful clinical work — and demand is significantly outpacing the supply of qualified practitioners globally.
keySkills: Assessing speech, language, voice, fluency, and swallowing across pediatric and adult populations
Designing and delivering evidence-based speech and language therapy programs
Conducting instrumental swallowing assessments including videofluoroscopy interpretation
Using augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices with non-speaking individuals
Applying motor speech therapy techniques for dysarthria and apraxia of speech
Providing early language intervention and parent coaching for young children with communication delays
Documenting treatment goals, session notes, and outcome measures in clinical records
opportunities: Pediatric speech therapist in a school, early intervention service, or children's hospital
Adult SLP in a hospital stroke unit or neurology rehabilitation team
Community SLP working with developmental, intellectual disability, or autism populations
SLP in a private practice specializing in stuttering or voice disorders
Research SLP in a university or clinical research center
SLP working with AAC and assistive technology for individuals with complex communication needs
verificationNote: Speech-language pathology practice requires country-specific licensing and registration; scope of practice and registration examinations vary by region.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research SLP degree programs and entry requirements in your country. Get volunteer or work experience with clinical populations — children with developmental conditions or adults in rehabilitation. Confirm your interest spans both pediatric and adult areas.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study linguistics, anatomy, neurology, and speech pathology clinical practice. Complete supervised clinical placements across pediatric, adult, and hospital settings. Pass registration assessments.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Begin practice with structured clinical supervision as a newly registered SLP. Develop caseload management and clinical reasoning across presentations. Identify specialist areas — pediatric language, adult neurological, or AAC.

title: Clinical Psychology
summary: Help people understand and change their own minds. One of the most human and genuinely impactful disciplines in all of healthcare — and one of the most demanding to qualify in.
description: Clinical psychologists assess, diagnose, and treat mental health conditions using psychological therapies including CBT, DBT, EMDR, and psychodynamic approaches. You work with people experiencing depression, anxiety, trauma, OCD, psychosis, eating disorders, chronic pain, and a wide range of other conditions. The path to becoming a clinical psychologist is long — you need an undergraduate degree in psychology, relevant clinical experience, and then a doctorate or professional training program that is highly competitive. Day to day, you carry a complex caseload, deliver therapy sessions, conduct psychological assessments, consult with teams, and contribute to service design. It is intellectually and emotionally demanding work that requires sustained personal resilience.
keySkills: Delivering evidence-based psychological therapies including CBT, DBT, ACT, and EMDR
Conducting structured psychological assessments and formulating complex presentations
Managing a clinical caseload safely including risk assessment and safeguarding decisions
Working within a multidisciplinary team in clinical, hospital, or community settings
Consulting and providing psychological advice to other professionals about their clients
Conducting clinical research and applying an evidence-based approach to therapy delivery
Writing detailed psychological assessment reports and therapy outcome summaries
opportunities: Clinical psychologist in a community mental health team
Hospital psychologist in a medical, neurological, or oncology setting
Forensic psychologist in a prison, secure hospital, or court service
Child psychologist in a child and adolescent mental health service (CAMHS)
Private practice clinical psychologist offering direct therapy services
Academic clinical psychologist combining research and clinical teaching
