keySkills: Designing and analyzing EV powertrain components including battery packs, motors, and inverters
Applying vehicle dynamics principles to suspension, steering, and handling design
Using CAD and simulation tools (CATIA, ANSYS, MATLAB/Simulink) for vehicle system design
Understanding battery cell chemistry, thermal behavior, and BMS design fundamentals
Applying automotive functional safety standards (ISO 26262) to safety-critical system design
Testing and validating vehicle systems from bench testing through to vehicle-level validation
Working within automotive quality and development processes (APQP, FMEA, control plans)
opportunities: EV powertrain engineer at an electric vehicle manufacturer or Tier 1 supplier
Battery engineer at a cell manufacturer or battery pack development company
Vehicle dynamics engineer at an automotive OEM or performance vehicle company
Automotive controls engineer developing software for propulsion or chassis systems
Homologation and type approval engineer at a vehicle manufacturer or regulatory body
Charging infrastructure engineer at an EV charging network company

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research automotive engineering or mechanical engineering degree programs with an automotive specialization. Understand that EV engineering increasingly requires both mechanical and electrical knowledge — plan to develop both.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study mechanical engineering fundamentals alongside automotive-specific modules in powertrain, dynamics, and vehicle design. Develop simulation skills in MATLAB/Simulink. Pursue internships at OEMs or Tier 1 suppliers — the automotive sector recruits heavily from placement students.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for graduate engineer positions at automotive OEMs, Tier 1 suppliers, or EV startups. Battery, power electronics, and software integration roles are the highest-demand areas in 2026.

title: Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering
summary: Optimize the systems that make things at scale. Cutting waste, improving output, and keeping production lines running — the engineering discipline behind every physical product that ships reliably.
description: Industrial and manufacturing engineers design, improve, and optimize the processes, systems, and facilities that produce goods. You apply engineering analysis, operations research, lean manufacturing, and ergonomics to make production systems faster, cheaper, safer, and less wasteful. Day to day, you might be mapping a production value stream to identify bottlenecks, designing a new workstation layout to reduce operator strain, implementing a statistical process control system, or simulating a new manufacturing line before it is physically installed. The discipline is highly applied and spans automotive, aerospace, electronics, pharmaceuticals, food, and consumer goods manufacturing. Lean, Six Sigma, and simulation tools are central to the role.
keySkills: Applying Lean manufacturing principles including value stream mapping, 5S, and kaizen improvement
Using Six Sigma tools for statistical process control and defect reduction
Designing production line layouts and ergonomic workstations using simulation tools
Calculating capacity, cycle times, and throughput rates for manufacturing planning
Implementing quality management systems aligned with ISO 9001 or IATF 16949
Analyzing machine downtime and applying OEE metrics to identify equipment improvement priorities
Leading cross-functional improvement projects with manufacturing, quality, and supply chain teams
opportunities: Manufacturing engineer at an automotive or electronics production facility
Process improvement engineer implementing Lean and Six Sigma programs
Operations engineer at a pharmaceutical or food manufacturing company
Industrial engineer at a logistics or fulfillment center optimizing throughput
Production planning engineer managing capacity and scheduling at a manufacturer
Quality engineer applying statistical methods to defect reduction and process control

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research industrial engineering or manufacturing engineering degree programs. Confirm mathematics and statistics prerequisites. Work experience in a manufacturing environment before or during your degree builds practical context significantly.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study operations research, manufacturing processes, quality engineering, supply chain, and Lean/Six Sigma. Develop simulation and data analysis skills. Industrial placement is highly recommended — manufacturing employers recruit heavily from their placement cohorts.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for graduate manufacturing or process improvement engineer roles at production companies in automotive, pharmaceuticals, or electronics. Six Sigma Green Belt certification significantly improves entry competitiveness.

title: Electrical Engineering
summary: Work with power, electronics, and the systems that run everything from homes to satellites to electric grids. The foundational engineering discipline of the electrified world.
description: Electrical engineers design and develop the electrical systems, power infrastructure, electronic devices, and control systems that modern civilization depends on. The field spans power systems (generation, transmission, and distribution), electronics (integrated circuits, sensors, and communications hardware), control systems (automation and feedback systems), and telecommunications (wireless and network infrastructure). Day to day, an electrical engineer might be designing a power distribution board for a building, developing firmware for a microcontroller-based control system, modeling an electric grid for stability analysis, or designing RF circuits for a wireless device. The field increasingly intersects with software as electrical systems become programmable and data-driven.
keySkills: Designing power distribution systems including switchgear, transformers, and protection systems
Analyzing circuits using Kirchhoff's laws, Thevenin equivalents, and phasors
Designing and simulating analogue and digital electronic circuits using SPICE or Multisim
Programming embedded systems and microcontrollers for control and data acquisition applications
Applying control theory including PID design and state-space methods to dynamic system control
Understanding electrical safety standards and applying them to installation and equipment design
Using test and measurement equipment including oscilloscopes, spectrum analyzers, and power meters
opportunities: Power systems engineer at a utility company or grid operator
Electronics design engineer at a technology hardware company
Control systems engineer in process control, automation, or robotics
Electrical design engineer at a building services or infrastructure consultancy
Embedded systems engineer combining electrical and software engineering skills
RF and communications engineer at a telecommunications or satellite company

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research accredited electrical or electronic engineering degree programs. Confirm strong mathematics and physics performance. Understand the breadth of the field — power, electronics, and controls lead to very different career destinations.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study circuit theory, electronics, electromagnetism, power systems, control, and signal processing. Develop practical laboratory skills alongside theoretical study. Industrial placement provides essential industry context.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for graduate electrical engineer roles in your target sector. Power, renewable energy, and embedded systems are among the highest-demand areas in 2026. Work toward Chartered Engineer status through your professional institution.

title: Chemical Engineering
summary: Scale up chemistry into industrial processes. Energy, pharmaceuticals, food production, and materials manufacturing at real-world scale — where chemistry meets engineering rigor.
description: Chemical engineers design and operate the industrial processes that convert raw materials into useful products at scale — pharmaceuticals, fuels, plastics, food and beverages, fertilizers, and specialty chemicals. You apply chemistry, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, mass and heat transfer, reaction engineering, and process control to design plants and optimize production. Day to day, a process engineer at a pharmaceutical company might be designing a chemical synthesis route and the equipment to run it safely at scale; a refinery engineer might be optimizing separation processes for fuel production; an environmental engineer might be designing waste treatment systems. Chemical engineers are among the highest-paid engineering graduates because the industries they serve — oil and gas, pharmaceuticals, chemicals — are capital-intensive and technically demanding.
keySkills: Applying mass and energy balance to design and troubleshoot chemical process systems
Designing unit operations including reactors, distillation columns, heat exchangers, and separators
Using process simulation software (Aspen Plus, HYSYS) to model and optimize plant design
Applying thermodynamics and reaction kinetics to process design and optimization
Understanding HAZOP, COSHH, and process safety management for chemical process industries
Scaling up laboratory processes to pilot and full industrial plant scale
Applying statistical process control and process analytical technology in pharmaceutical manufacturing
opportunities: Process engineer at a pharmaceutical or fine chemicals manufacturing company
Petroleum or refinery engineer at an oil and gas processing facility
Environmental process engineer at a water treatment or waste management company
Technical sales engineer at a specialty chemicals or process equipment company
Food process engineer at a food and beverage manufacturing company
Chemical plant engineer at a large industrial chemical production facility

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research accredited chemical engineering degree programs. Confirm strong mathematics, chemistry, and physics foundations. The degree is demanding and mathematically intensive — entry requirements are typically high.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, heat and mass transfer, reaction engineering, and process design. Complete a plant design project in your final year. Industrial placement — especially in pharmaceuticals or petrochemicals — is highly recommended.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for graduate process or chemical engineer roles in pharmaceuticals, oil and gas, chemicals, or food. These industries have well-established graduate programs. Chartership through IChemE is the long-term professional credential.

title: Nuclear Engineering
summary: Design systems that harness nuclear energy — from power generation to medical imaging to decommissioning legacy infrastructure. A field in significant resurgence as clean energy demand grows.
description: Nuclear engineers design, develop, and operate systems that use nuclear reactions — power reactors, medical imaging and treatment systems, nuclear propulsion, and the decommissioning of legacy nuclear infrastructure. The civilian nuclear industry is experiencing a major revival driven by clean energy demand — small modular reactors (SMRs) are moving from concept to construction in multiple countries, and the nuclear workforce requirement is growing faster than the training pipeline can fill it. Day to day, a nuclear power engineer might be analyzing reactor thermal-hydraulic behavior, overseeing fuel management planning, managing a safety case review, or coordinating a complex decommissioning project. Safety culture is not optional in this field — it is the organizing principle of every decision.
keySkills: Applying nuclear physics principles including fission, decay chains, and neutron transport
Analyzing reactor thermal-hydraulics and safety systems using specialized simulation codes
Understanding and applying nuclear regulatory frameworks and safety case requirements
Performing shielding analysis and radiation protection design for nuclear facilities
Managing nuclear waste classification and disposal in compliance with regulatory requirements
Applying quality assurance and nuclear safety culture principles in all engineering work
Conducting safety analysis and contributing to nuclear safety case documentation
opportunities: Nuclear engineer at a power utility operating nuclear power stations
SMR development engineer at a small modular reactor design and construction company
Radiation protection advisor at a nuclear facility or hospital radiotherapy unit
Decommissioning engineer managing the safe dismantling of legacy nuclear infrastructure
Nuclear safety case engineer at a regulatory body or nuclear consultancy
Medical physics engineer working with radiation therapy and nuclear medicine equipment
verificationNote: Nuclear engineering roles require country-specific security clearance and regulatory authorization; requirements for safety-critical nuclear work vary significantly by jurisdiction.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research nuclear engineering or physics/engineering with nuclear specialization degree programs. Confirm strong mathematics and physics foundations. Understand the security clearance requirements that apply to nuclear roles in your country.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study nuclear physics, reactor engineering, radiation protection, thermal-hydraulics, and nuclear materials. Gain practical experience through placements with nuclear operators, regulators, or national laboratories.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for graduate nuclear engineer roles at power utilities, SMR companies, or decommissioning contractors. Obtain the security clearances required for your role. Work toward Chartered Engineer status through relevant professional institutions.

title: Aerospace Engineering
summary: Design aircraft and spacecraft. One of the most technically demanding engineering disciplines — with among the highest stakes of any profession and a commercial space sector in rapid acceleration.
description: Aerospace engineers design and develop aircraft, spacecraft, satellites, propulsion systems, and the supporting ground systems. The field divides into aeronautical engineering (aircraft) and astronautical engineering (spacecraft), though the disciplines overlap significantly in thermodynamics, structures, and systems engineering. You apply aerodynamics, structural mechanics, propulsion, avionics, and control theory to create vehicles that operate in some of the harshest environments imaginable — where failure has catastrophic consequences. Day to day, an aerodynamics engineer might be running CFD simulations on a new wing design; a propulsion engineer might be analyzing combustion characteristics in a turbofan; a structures engineer might be designing a composite fuselage section. The commercial space sector has expanded the range of employers significantly beyond traditional defence and aerospace primes.
keySkills: Applying aerodynamic principles and running CFD analysis to evaluate aircraft and spacecraft designs
Designing and analyzing aerospace structural components under static and dynamic loading
Understanding propulsion systems including gas turbines, rocket motors, and electric propulsion
Applying systems engineering methodology to complex, multi-disciplinary aerospace projects
Working with aerospace material specifications including aluminium alloys, titanium, and composites
Navigating aerospace certification frameworks including EASA CS-25 and FAA FAR Part 25
Performing mass budget analysis and space systems engineering for satellite and spacecraft design
opportunities: Aerodynamics engineer at an aircraft manufacturer or defense contractor
Spacecraft systems engineer at a commercial space company or national space agency
Propulsion engineer at a jet engine or rocket motor development organization
Avionics engineer developing flight control and navigation systems
Structural engineer at an aerospace composite structures manufacturing company
Satellite engineer at a small satellite manufacturer or launch services company

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research accredited aerospace engineering degree programs. Confirm very strong mathematics and physics performance — aerospace has among the highest entry requirements of any engineering discipline. Understand that most roles require security clearance.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study aerodynamics, structural mechanics, propulsion, flight dynamics, and systems engineering. Develop CAD and CFD skills from early in the degree. Summer internships at aerospace companies are competitive but transformative.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for graduate aerospace engineer roles at aircraft manufacturers, defense prime contractors, or commercial space companies. Security clearance eligibility is a practical requirement for most roles in the sector.

title: Environmental Engineering
summary: Engineer solutions to pollution, waste, and water quality. Applying engineering discipline to the sustainability crisis — and one of the most consequential technical careers of the next century.
description: Environmental engineers design systems and solutions that protect the natural environment and human health from pollution and waste — water and wastewater treatment plants, contaminated land remediation systems, air quality control equipment, solid waste management facilities, and environmental monitoring networks. You apply chemical, biological, and physical engineering principles to prevent or reverse environmental damage. Day to day, you might be designing a bioreactor for treating industrial wastewater, modeling the fate of a chemical contaminant in groundwater, specifying air pollution control equipment for a factory, or conducting a technical assessment of a contaminated site. This is engineering with direct environmental and public health outcomes — and the regulatory and sustainability drivers for this work are intensifying.
keySkills: Designing water and wastewater treatment processes including biological, physical, and chemical treatment
Modeling contaminant fate and transport in soil, groundwater, and surface water systems
Specifying and sizing air pollution control equipment for industrial and municipal sources
Conducting environmental impact assessments for infrastructure and industrial projects
Applying environmental regulations and discharge standards to process design decisions
Designing contaminated land investigation and remediation strategies
Using environmental modeling software for air dispersion, groundwater flow, and flood risk analysis
opportunities: Water engineer at a utility company designing treatment and distribution systems
Contaminated land consultant at an environmental engineering consultancy
Air quality engineer at an industrial plant or environmental regulator
Environmental compliance engineer at a manufacturing or processing facility
Waste management engineer designing solid waste infrastructure at a local authority
Environmental project manager at a consultancy delivering remediation and sustainability projects

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research environmental engineering or civil engineering with environmental specialization degree programs. Confirm mathematics, chemistry, and biology foundations. Understand the distinction between environmental science and environmental engineering.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study water and wastewater engineering, air quality, contaminated land, environmental chemistry, and process engineering. Complete design projects in treatment systems or remediation. Industry placement at an environmental consultancy is highly recommended.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for graduate environmental engineer roles at water utilities, environmental consultancies, or industrial companies with environmental departments. Work toward Chartered status through ICE, IChemE, or equivalent professional institution.

title: Renewable Energy Engineering
summary: Design solar, wind, battery, and grid systems. The engineering challenge and the commercial opportunity of the entire 21st century — and a career growing faster than almost any other in engineering.
description: Renewable energy engineers design, develop, and optimize the solar, wind, hydropower, battery, and grid systems that are decarbonizing the global energy supply. The field is growing at a pace few engineering disciplines match — every major economy is deploying renewable capacity at scale, and the gap between ambition and engineering workforce is significant and widening. Day to day, a solar engineer might be designing a large-scale photovoltaic array, modeling energy yield, and specifying inverter and cabling systems; a wind energy engineer might be analyzing turbine loading data, optimizing blade pitch control, or managing a site assessment; a grid engineer might be modeling the stability impacts of high renewable penetration or designing battery storage systems for frequency regulation.
keySkills: Designing solar PV systems including site assessment, layout, shading analysis, and grid connection
Analyzing wind resources and turbine selection using WAsP or equivalent site modeling tools
Sizing battery energy storage systems for utility-scale and commercial applications
Applying power systems analysis to grid connection design and network stability assessment
Using SCADA and energy management systems for renewable plant monitoring and control
Conducting techno-economic analysis and financial modeling for renewable energy projects
Understanding planning, permitting, and grid code requirements for renewable energy development
opportunities: Solar PV design engineer at a renewable energy developer or EPC contractor
Wind energy engineer at a wind turbine manufacturer or offshore wind developer
Battery storage systems engineer at an energy storage technology company
Grid integration engineer at a transmission system operator or energy utility
Energy systems consultant at a renewable energy advisory firm
Offshore wind engineer specializing in foundation design or installation engineering

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research renewable energy engineering, electrical engineering, or energy systems degree programs. Confirm mathematics and physics foundations. Understand the intersection of electrical, mechanical, and environmental engineering that defines this field.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study power systems, electrical machines, resource assessment, energy storage, and renewable technology. Develop simulation and data analysis skills. The sector recruits heavily from internship programs at developers, manufacturers, and consultancies.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Apply for graduate roles at renewable energy developers, EPC contractors, or energy consultancies. Solar, offshore wind, and battery storage are experiencing the strongest growth in headcount and offer the most graduate entry opportunities.

title: Culinary Arts
summary: Master fire, knife, flavor, and timing. Professional kitchens are among the most demanding environments in any field — and they produce something genuinely beautiful.
description: Culinary professionals create food for restaurants, hotels, catering companies, private clients, and the growing world of food content and media. The kitchen hierarchy is structured and demanding — you start at the bottom, learn from those above you, and progress by developing technique, speed, and creative palate over years of intense daily practice. Day to day, a chef might be preparing a mise en place for 80 covers, developing a new tasting menu, managing a section during service, or working recipe development for a food company. The industry has a well-documented issue with long hours and mental health — awareness and working conditions are improving but the culture remains demanding. Those who succeed combine genuine passion for food with the discipline and physical resilience the environment requires.
keySkills: Applying classical French and international culinary techniques to a professional cooking standard
Executing mise en place efficiently and managing prep timelines under service pressure
Understanding flavor profiles, seasoning, and palate development across different cuisines
Managing a kitchen section independently during service with speed, accuracy, and consistency
Developing and costing new menus with portion control, waste reduction, and profitability awareness
Maintaining food hygiene, allergen management, and HACCP compliance in food preparation
Working effectively in a brigade team environment under pressure and hierarchical direction
opportunities: Commis chef or chef de partie in a restaurant kitchen at any star level
Head chef or executive chef in a hotel, restaurant group, or private club
Pastry chef specializing in desserts, bread, and patisserie production
Private or personal chef for individual clients or corporate catering
Food content creator combining culinary skill with digital media for brand and social work
Recipe developer and food stylist for cookbooks, food magazines, and advertising

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Complete a culinary arts qualification or begin work as a kitchen porter or commis chef. Cooking school provides technique; real kitchen work provides speed and resilience. Both are essential. Work in the best kitchen you can access.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Work your way through multiple stations in a kitchen. Work in different types of operations — fine dining, high volume, different cuisines. Move kitchens deliberately to broaden your skills. Stage (work experience) at excellent restaurants if possible.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Culinary careers progress through demonstrated ability in the kitchen — there is no single credential. The CV that matters is the list of kitchens you have worked in and what you learned there. Specialize or broaden based on where your strengths and passion align.

title: Hospitality and Tourism Management
summary: Create the experiences people save money and plan months for. The world's largest service industry — one that directly shapes quality of life and cultural exchange at global scale.
description: Hospitality and tourism managers plan, deliver, and improve the experiences of guests at hotels, resorts, airlines, travel companies, restaurants, cruise lines, and visitor attractions. You manage operations, staff, service standards, revenue, and customer relationships across environments where the margin between memorable and forgettable is often razor thin. Day to day, a hotel general manager might be reviewing occupancy forecasts, handling a guest complaint, leading a team briefing, and meeting with a corporate account — all before noon. Tourism managers at destination organizations might be planning marketing campaigns, managing tour operator relationships, or developing sustainable tourism strategies. This industry is people-intensive and culture-defining.
keySkills: Managing hospitality operations including rooms, food and beverage, and front-of-house across a guest property
Applying revenue management principles to optimize yield across occupancy, rate, and channel mix
Leading and developing service teams in high-pressure, guest-facing environments
Handling guest complaints and service recovery with professionalism and genuine care
Understanding tourism distribution — OTAs, GDS, tour operators, and direct booking channels
Managing financial performance including P&L, budgeting, and cost control in a hospitality operation
Developing and maintaining service standards and quality management systems
opportunities: Hotel manager at a branded or independent property
Front office or operations manager at a city hotel or resort
Revenue manager optimizing pricing and distribution at a hotel group
Tour operator product manager developing and selling travel packages
Events and conference manager at a hotel or venue
Destination management organization officer promoting tourism to a region or country

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Get into a hospitality operation in any capacity — the industry promotes from within and values demonstrated aptitude over qualifications. Front-line experience in reception, food service, or events is the starting point.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Move through departments to develop operational breadth. A hospitality management degree or diploma can run concurrently with work. International experience is highly valued — work in a different country if possible.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Target supervisory and management trainee roles at hotel groups, resort operators, or tourism organizations. Revenue management and general management are the highest-earning long-term tracks in hospitality.

title: Skilled Trades (Electrician, Plumber, HVAC)
summary: Keep the physical world functioning. Skilled, licensed, essential, and increasingly well-compensated as shortages grow — and a career that cannot be automated or offshored.
description: Electricians, plumbers, HVAC technicians, and other licensed tradespeople install, maintain, and repair the infrastructure systems that make buildings habitable and functional. Electricians wire buildings for power, lighting, and communications; plumbers install and maintain water supply, drainage, and heating systems; HVAC technicians install and service climate control and ventilation systems. Training is through apprenticeship — combining paid work in a trade business with technical education over several years. Licensing is legally required in most countries, and the qualification process is both practical and technically rigorous. In 2026, skilled trades shortages are significant in most developed economies — demand is high, wages are rising, and the work cannot be sent offshore.
keySkills: Interpreting electrical wiring diagrams, plumbing schematics, or HVAC design drawings for installation work
Installing, testing, and commissioning systems to manufacturer specifications and regulatory standards
Diagnosing faults in existing systems using appropriate testing equipment and methodical troubleshooting
Applying building and safety regulations relevant to your trade and jurisdiction
Working safely at height, in confined spaces, and with hazardous materials following safety protocols
Communicating clearly with clients and contractors on site about work progress and issues
Maintaining accurate job records, material records, and completion documentation
opportunities: Qualified electrician with a trade contractor or running an independent business
Plumber specializing in residential or commercial new build or maintenance
HVAC installation and service engineer at a commercial facilities management company
Renewable energy systems installer specializing in solar PV and heat pumps
Maintenance electrician or plumber at a large commercial or industrial facility
Site services manager overseeing trade contractors on a construction project
verificationNote: Skilled trade licensing requirements vary significantly by country, state, and trade; verify local apprenticeship programs, examination requirements, and licensing bodies before starting.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Entry
journeyPhases.focus: Research apprenticeship programs in your chosen trade and region. Apply to trade contractors who run formal apprenticeship programs. Entry requirements are modest — aptitude for practical work and basic mathematics matter most.

journeyPhases.name: Apprenticeship
journeyPhases.focus: Complete your apprenticeship — working in the trade full-time while attending college for technical training. The combination of on-site experience and classroom instruction is the defining phase of trade qualification.

journeyPhases.name: Qualification and Licensing
journeyPhases.focus: Sit licensing examinations and obtain your trade license. Begin working as a qualified tradesperson. Consider specialization in renewable energy systems, data center infrastructure, or commercial HVAC — these carry significant pay premiums.

title: Real Estate Agency
summary: Help people make one of the largest financial decisions of their lives. Market knowledge, negotiation, and genuine human trust at the center of every transaction.
description: Real estate agents and brokers facilitate the buying, selling, and renting of residential and commercial property — acting as intermediaries between buyers and sellers or landlords and tenants. You value properties, market them, conduct viewings, negotiate offers, and guide clients through the legal and financial process of completing a transaction. The income model is commission-based in most markets, which means earnings are directly tied to performance — high performers earn significantly above average; average performance pays moderately. The job is fundamentally relationship-driven: clients choose the agent they trust, and reputation compounds over years of successful transactions. Licensing is required in virtually every market and typically involves completing a course and passing a state or national examination.
keySkills: Valuing residential and commercial properties using comparable sales analysis
Marketing properties effectively across portals, social media, and a personal network
Conducting property viewings and communicating property features with expertise
Negotiating between buyers and sellers to reach agreed terms on price and conditions
Managing transaction pipelines from offer acceptance through to legal completion
Building and maintaining a client database and referral network for repeat and referred business
Understanding property law, conveyancing process, and mortgage basics to guide clients accurately
opportunities: Residential estate agent at an independent or branded agency
Commercial property agent specializing in office, retail, or industrial lettings
Luxury property specialist at a high-end residential agency
Property developer's sales agent managing new build scheme sales
Lettings agent managing a rental portfolio for landlords
Self-employed real estate agent building an independent client book
verificationNote: Real estate agency requires country-specific licensing; examination requirements, continuing education, and regulatory oversight vary significantly by region and state.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Research real estate licensing requirements in your country or state. Complete the required pre-license coursework and sit the licensing examination. Understand the local property market — prices, demand, typical buyer profiles — before your first client.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Join an established agency to learn the business under experienced agents. The first year is about learning how deals work, building your network, and developing the market knowledge that creates client confidence.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Build a track record of completed transactions and client testimonials. The best agents grow primarily through referrals — your reputation is built transaction by transaction. Specializing in a neighborhood or property type builds expertise that clients recognize.

title: Construction Management
summary: Oversee the projects that physically build cities. Coordinating teams, budgets, timelines, and safety on everything from homes to hospitals to skyscrapers.
description: Construction managers plan and deliver building projects — coordinating architects, engineers, trade contractors, suppliers, and client stakeholders to complete a project on time, on budget, and to the specified quality. You manage contracts, health and safety, procurement, program scheduling, and the daily decisions that keep a complex multi-party project moving forward. Day to day, you might be running a site progress meeting, reviewing a subcontractor's variation claim, coordinating the phasing of a fit-out with an occupying tenant, or escalating a structural issue to the project engineer. The role requires both technical understanding of construction methods and the commercial and interpersonal skills to manage contracts and relationships. It is a career with significant earning potential at senior levels and broad options — residential, commercial, infrastructure, and specialist sectors all need construction managers.
keySkills: Programming and scheduling construction projects using Microsoft Project, Primavera, or ASTA
Managing construction contracts (JCT, NEC, or equivalent) including variations and claims
Coordinating design information from architects and engineers for contractor use
Overseeing site health and safety compliance and conducting regular site safety inspections
Managing subcontractor packages from procurement through to completion and final account
Controlling project cost budgets and managing change with accurate cost impact assessment
Communicating project progress, risk, and issues clearly to client and senior management
opportunities: Site manager at a residential or commercial contractor
Project manager at a main contractor delivering medium-to-large construction schemes
Construction manager at a developer overseeing projects from their client side
Quantity surveyor managing cost planning, tendering, and final accounts
Contracts manager overseeing multiple concurrent projects within a contractor's portfolio
Development manager at a housebuilder or commercial property developer

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Decide your entry route — a construction management degree or starting in a trade or site-based role and progressing upward. Both are valid; the site-based route takes longer but provides irreplaceable practical understanding.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Gain site experience across different project types. Learn contracts, programming tools, and cost management. CIOB membership exams or a RICS quantity surveying route provide structured professional development alongside work.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Target junior project or site manager roles at main contractors or developer client teams. The path from site to project director is well-defined and meritocratic — performance on site creates advancement.

title: Beauty and Cosmetology
summary: Work directly with people to help them look and feel their best. A creative, client-centered, and deeply personal career — and a growing industry.
description: Cosmetologists, hairdressers, estheticians, nail technicians, and beauty therapists provide appearance and well-being services directly to clients — haircuts, coloring, skincare treatments, nail care, makeup artistry, waxing, and massage. The work is physically demanding (hours on your feet) and emotionally rewarding — clients often develop long-term relationships with their stylist or therapist built on trust and comfort. Most beauty and cosmetology roles require a vocational qualification and government license in most countries. Career paths include working in salons, spas, film and television sets, fashion editorial, bridal services, and building an independent clientele. Social media has opened new opportunities for beauty professionals to build personal brands and reach new clients directly.
keySkills: Cutting and styling hair across different hair types, textures, and client preferences
Applying hair coloring techniques including balayage, highlights, and permanent color
Performing skincare treatments including facials, chemical peels, and microdermabrasion
Applying makeup for bridal, editorial, film, television, and commercial contexts
Building and maintaining long-term client relationships through consistent service quality
Managing retail product recommendations and upselling services professionally and genuinely
Maintaining hygiene, sterilization, and safety standards required for licensed practice
opportunities: Hair stylist or colorist at a salon
Esthetician or beauty therapist at a spa or skin clinic
Makeup artist for weddings, film, television, and fashion editorial
Nail technician at a nail salon or mobile nail services business
Brand educator or ambassador representing a professional beauty brand
Salon owner or independent booth renter building a personal client book
verificationNote: Cosmetology and beauty therapy licensing requirements vary significantly by country and state; required training hours, examinations, and renewal requirements differ by region and specialty.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Enroll in an accredited cosmetology or beauty therapy program. Complete the required training hours for your specialty. The fundamentals — technique, hygiene, and client communication — are established in this phase.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Sit your licensing examination and obtain your state or national license. Assist in a salon or practice under supervision to build speed, client management skills, and a personal style that differentiates you.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Build a portfolio of your work through social media — Instagram and TikTok are effective platforms for beauty professionals. Start building your client book. Consider specialization in color, skincare, or makeup for higher earning potential.

title: Sports Science and Coaching
summary: Apply physiology, psychology, and biomechanics to athletic performance. Behind every elite result is a sports science team — and behind every effective coach is a scientific framework.
description: Sports scientists and coaches apply exercise physiology, biomechanics, sports psychology, and performance analysis to improve athletic performance. Sports scientists work in high-performance sport environments — national institutes, professional clubs, and elite academies — collecting and analyzing data on training load, movement patterns, physiological markers, and psychological readiness. Coaches apply this knowledge directly in athlete development, designing training programs and delivering technical instruction. The two roles overlap significantly at the high-performance level. Day to day, a strength and conditioning coach might be designing periodization programs and running gym sessions; a performance analyst might be reviewing competition footage to identify tactical patterns; a sports psychologist might be working individually with athletes on confidence and mental preparation.
keySkills: Designing periodized training programs for strength, conditioning, and sport-specific preparation
Measuring and monitoring athlete load using GPS, heart rate, RPE, and recovery metrics
Applying biomechanical analysis to technique assessment and injury risk reduction
Using performance analysis software (Hudl, Nacsport, Catapult) to review and present athletic data
Applying sport psychology principles to mental performance, motivation, and resilience
Delivering individual and group coaching sessions with clear technical instruction and feedback
Communicating performance data and recommendations to athletes, coaches, and medical staff
opportunities: Strength and conditioning coach at a professional sports club
Performance analyst at a national sports institute or elite academy
Sport science lecturer at a university or sports college
Athletic coach at a national governing body or high-performance center
Performance consultant working independently with individual elite athletes
Community sports development officer delivering participation programs

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Develop a sports science or exercise science knowledge base through formal study or self-study. Begin coaching or performance analysis work in any sporting context — community, school, or amateur club. Applied experience from day one matters.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Complete a sports science degree or coaching qualification at national governing body level. Work in a performance environment — unpaid if necessary initially. UKSCA accreditation (S&C), PFSA (performance analysis), or BPS (psychology) credentials build professional credibility.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Target assistant S&C, performance analyst, or development coach roles at professional clubs or national institutes. High-performance sports is relationship-driven — professional network matters as much as credentials.

title: Personal Training and Fitness
summary: Guide people through physical transformation. Increasingly evidence-based, increasingly in demand, and deeply personal work that changes how people live and feel in their bodies.
description: Personal trainers design and deliver individualized exercise programs for clients seeking to improve their fitness, body composition, athletic performance, or health. You assess clients' starting points, set goals, design progressive training programs, coach technique, monitor progress, and provide the accountability and motivation that makes the difference between a plan and an outcome. Modern personal training is increasingly evidence-based — the most effective trainers combine understanding of exercise physiology, nutrition, behavior change, and psychology with practical coaching ability. The business model is typically self-employed — trainers work in gyms, online, in clients' homes, or run their own studios. Building and retaining a client base is as important as coaching skill.
keySkills: Conducting client needs assessments including movement screening, goal setting, and health history
Designing progressive resistance and cardiovascular training programs for different client goals
Coaching exercise technique with clear, safe, and effective cueing for both novice and experienced clients
Applying behavior change principles to support clients through motivation drops and plateaus
Monitoring and adjusting training programs based on client progress, recovery, and feedback
Understanding basic sports nutrition principles and knowing the limits of scope of practice
Marketing personal training services and building a sustainable client base and retention system
opportunities: Personal trainer at a gym chain or boutique fitness studio
Online personal trainer building a remote coaching practice
Specialist trainer focusing on pre/postnatal, older adults, or rehabilitation clients
Gym manager or fitness director at a health club or corporate wellness facility
Group fitness instructor delivering classes in strength, HIIT, yoga, or cycling
Corporate wellness consultant delivering fitness programs in workplace settings

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Complete a Level 3 Personal Trainer certification (UK) or NASM, ACE, or NSCA-CPT certification (US or internationally recognized). Learn how gyms and the fitness industry work. Begin training real clients under supervision.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Build your first client base through floor work at a gym, social media, or referrals. Develop specialization in an area of genuine interest — strength, fat loss, sports performance, or rehabilitation — to differentiate your services.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Build client testimonials and transformation case studies. Develop an online presence. Pursue continuing education in nutrition, behavior change, or a specialist population. The most successful trainers invest heavily in both client results and their own education.

title: Health and Wellness Coaching
summary: Guide people toward sustainable changes in how they live, sleep, eat, and move. The line between coaching and healthcare is narrowing — and the demand for evidence-based wellness support is growing.
description: Health and wellness coaches support individuals in making lasting lifestyle changes — improving sleep, managing stress, increasing physical activity, improving dietary habits, and building sustainable daily routines that support long-term health. Unlike clinical professionals, coaches do not diagnose or treat medical conditions — they help clients identify their own goals, build motivation, overcome barriers, and develop the habits and self-awareness that produce lasting change. The profession operates in corporate wellness programs, private practice, digital health platforms, and alongside clinical teams. Coaching effectiveness depends primarily on interpersonal skill, understanding of behavior change science, and the ability to support without prescribing.
keySkills: Applying behavior change models including motivational interviewing, ACT, and habit formation science
Conducting structured coaching conversations that support client self-discovery and goal setting
Building personalized wellness plans addressing sleep, movement, nutrition, and stress management
Working within scope of practice and making appropriate referrals to clinical professionals
Using digital health tracking tools and apps to support client accountability and monitoring
Facilitating group coaching programs for corporate wellness or online communities
Building and managing a coaching practice including client acquisition, retention, and pricing
opportunities: Corporate wellness coach delivering programs to employees at large organizations
Independent health coach running a private practice online or locally
Digital health coach on a wellness platform or app serving a large user base
Integrative health coach working alongside GPs and clinical teams in primary care
Chronic disease wellness coach at a healthcare organization supporting lifestyle management
Group coaching facilitator running cohort-based wellness programs

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Complete an ICF-accredited health or life coaching certification. Learn the core coaching methodology — motivational interviewing, active listening, and goal-setting frameworks. Practice coaching on willing volunteers before taking paid clients.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Build a client base and develop your niche — stress management, sleep improvement, weight management, or corporate wellness are all distinct specializations. Study behavior change science and nutrition basics at an appropriate depth.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Document client outcomes and build testimonials. Develop online presence through content that demonstrates your approach and expertise. Apply for corporate wellness roles or digital coaching platform partnerships as a secondary income stream.

title: Event Management
summary: Produce the moments people remember for years. From concerts and corporate summits to weddings and sporting events — you make the complex feel effortless to everyone in the room.
description: Event managers plan, coordinate, and deliver events — managing every element from initial concept and venue selection through to on-the-day execution and post-event reporting. You juggle multiple workstreams simultaneously: client relationships, supplier contracts, budget management, marketing, logistics, staffing, and the thousand operational decisions that make an event run smoothly. Day to day, you might be negotiating an AV contract, reviewing a running order, managing a client's changing brief, or solving a catering issue 30 minutes before doors open. Events range from intimate corporate dinners to major international conferences and music festivals. The work is deadline-driven and high-pressure — and genuinely rewarding when it comes together.
keySkills: Planning and managing event timelines, run-of-shows, and logistics across multiple workstreams
Negotiating and managing supplier contracts for venues, catering, AV, production, and staffing
Managing event budgets with accurate forecasting, tracking, and variance reporting
Coordinating client relationships and translating briefs into detailed event specifications
Leading on-site event operations and managing teams and suppliers in real time
Applying health and safety, licensing, and risk assessment to event planning and delivery
Managing post-event evaluation, reporting, and stakeholder feedback processes
opportunities: Event coordinator at a corporate events agency
Wedding planner at an independent or hotel-based events company
Conference manager at a convention center or professional conference organizer
Festival operations manager at a music or cultural event organization
In-house events manager at a large corporation managing internal events calendar
Experiential marketing manager producing brand activation events for clients

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Volunteer or assist at events in any role — stewarding, registration, logistics. The event industry is experience-first. Understanding how events work from the inside before you manage them is essential.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Get into a coordinator role at an agency or in-house team. Learn to manage budgets, supplier relationships, and event timelines simultaneously. Take ownership of small events before building to larger, more complex ones.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Build a portfolio of delivered events with client testimonials. Apply for event manager or senior coordinator roles. Consider a CMP (Certified Meeting Professional) or DES certification for corporate and conference specialization.

title: Esports and Gaming Industry
summary: Work in competition management, broadcasting, analytics, or event production in one of the world's fastest-growing entertainment sectors.
description: The esports and gaming industry spans professional competitive gaming, live events, broadcasting, content creation, team and league management, sponsorship, analytics, and game publishing. Unlike professional players (whose careers are short and intensely competitive), the broader industry employs coaches, analysts, talent managers, event producers, broadcast technicians, casters, social media managers, and operations professionals — creating a diverse employment ecosystem. Day to day, an esports operations coordinator might be managing tournament brackets, coordinating with team managers, and overseeing venue logistics; a data analyst might be building performance models from competitive data; a broadcast producer might be managing a live multi-camera esports stream. The sector is professionalizing rapidly, with roles increasingly resembling traditional sports management and media careers.
keySkills: Understanding competitive game ecosystems, meta-game dynamics, and professional player performance
Managing esports tournament operations including bracket management, scheduling, and technical setup
Producing and coordinating live esports broadcasts including caster management and production workflow
Analyzing player and team performance data using game-specific analytics platforms
Building community engagement and audience development through social media and content strategy
Managing team or league stakeholder relationships including players, sponsors, and publishers
Applying traditional event management, project management, and marketing skills in the gaming context
opportunities: Esports event coordinator at a tournament organizer or publisher-run league
Performance analyst at a professional esports organization
Esports caster or host for competitive broadcasts
Community manager at a game studio or esports organization
Partnership and sponsorship manager at an esports team or league
Esports journalist or content creator covering the competitive gaming industry

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Develop deep knowledge of the esports ecosystem — competitive titles, organizations, leagues, and industry structure. Engage with the community through volunteering at local tournaments, creating content, or joining amateur organizational teams.

journeyPhases.name: Core Development
journeyPhases.focus: Build experience in your target role area — production, analytics, management, or media — through community events, content creation, or unpaid roles at small organizations. The esports industry rewards demonstrable passion and portfolio over formal credentials.

journeyPhases.name: Entry and Portfolio
journeyPhases.focus: Document your event experience, analytical work, or content portfolio. Apply for coordinator, analyst, or associate roles at esports organizations, game publishers, or broadcast companies. Transferable skills from event management or media careers are genuinely valued.

title: Early Childhood Education
summary: Shape people at the age when they are most impressionable. Research consistently shows this is the highest-leverage point in human development — and the most undervalued work in most societies.
description: Early childhood educators work with children from birth to around age 8 — in nurseries, childcare centers, preschools, kindergartens, and the early years of primary school. You design and deliver play-based learning experiences, support language development and social-emotional growth, observe and document developmental progress, and communicate regularly with parents and families. The work is physically active, emotionally present, and cognitively demanding — planning environments and activities that stimulate development without over-directing it requires deep understanding of child development. Qualification requirements vary enormously by country and setting — from short vocational certificates for nursery work to full teaching qualifications for kindergarten and reception class teaching.
keySkills: Designing play-based learning environments and activities that support developmental milestones
Observing, documenting, and assessing children's development across all domains
Supporting speech, language, and communication development through daily interaction and activity
Applying child safeguarding and protection frameworks in daily practice
Building positive, consistent, and secure relationships with young children
Communicating children's progress and development to parents and families clearly
Identifying and supporting children with additional needs or developmental delays
opportunities: Early years practitioner in a nursery or childcare center
Kindergarten or reception class teacher in a primary school
Family support worker providing home-based early intervention
Forest school or outdoor education practitioner
EYFS lead coordinating the early years provision across a school
Early childhood education lecturer at a college or university
verificationNote: Early childhood education qualification and registration requirements vary significantly by country and setting type; verify local requirements for childcare, nursery, and classroom roles before starting a program.

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Understand qualification requirements in your country and setting type. Gain work experience in a childcare or early years setting before committing to a training program. Caring about children is necessary but not sufficient — the pedagogy is demanding.

journeyPhases.name: Core Training
journeyPhases.focus: Complete the relevant qualification for your target role — Level 3 certificate for nursery practice in the UK, Early Childhood Education degree or ECE diploma in other countries. Practical placement experience is the most important component.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Begin in a registered childcare or early years setting. For teaching in primary school settings, a full teaching qualification and registration is required. Consider specialization in special educational needs, outdoor learning, or family support.

title: EdTech and Learning Design
summary: Build the tools and curricula that change how people learn. Technology-led education at a scale no classroom ever reached — and one of the few technology sectors where purpose and product genuinely align.
description: EdTech and learning design professionals create the digital products, platforms, curricula, and experiences that make learning more effective, accessible, and engaging. Learning designers build course content and instructional frameworks — applying cognitive science principles to structure knowledge transfer. EdTech product builders create the platforms, adaptive learning systems, assessment tools, and AI tutors that deliver learning at scale. Day to day, a learning designer might be structuring a 12-week professional development course, writing learning objectives, and commissioning video content; an EdTech product manager might be defining the roadmap for an AI feedback tool, working with engineers on implementation, and reviewing learner engagement data. The best EdTech work combines deep understanding of how people learn with rigorous product and content discipline.
keySkills: Applying instructional design principles including learning objectives, scaffolding, and spaced repetition
Designing online courses using authoring tools like Articulate Storyline or Rise
Building and analyzing learner engagement data to improve course completion and outcomes
Applying cognitive load theory and multimedia learning principles to content design
Working with subject matter experts to convert knowledge into structured learning experiences
Designing formative and summative assessments that accurately measure learning
Integrating AI tutoring, adaptive learning, and personalized learning pathways into EdTech products
opportunities: Learning designer at an online education platform or corporate training company
EdTech product manager at a learning technology startup
Instructional designer at a university designing online degree programs
Corporate learning and development specialist building internal training programs
EdTech content producer creating video-based learning experiences
Head of learning design at a professional skills or bootcamp company

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Study instructional design fundamentals and the science of how people learn. Learn one authoring tool (Articulate Rise is the most accessible starting point). Develop a clear view of whether you are more drawn to content design or product/technology.

journeyPhases.name: Core Skills
journeyPhases.focus: Design a complete learning experience — define objectives, structure content, build assessment, and evaluate outcomes. For EdTech product roles, combine instructional knowledge with product management or engineering skills.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Build a portfolio of designed learning experiences with documented outcome data. Target instructional designer or EdTech associate PM roles at online education companies, corporate training departments, or edtech startups.

title: Space Technology
summary: Build systems for the new era of commercial spaceflight, satellite infrastructure, and deep-space exploration. A field accelerating faster than any other — and opening up as commercial investment floods in.
description: Space technology professionals design, build, test, and operate the systems that function in space — satellites, launch vehicles, ground stations, spacecraft propulsion, communications payloads, and the software that controls them from Earth. The commercial space sector has expanded enormously since 2010: companies like SpaceX, Planet Labs, OneWeb, and hundreds of startups have created a new generation of employment opportunities beyond the traditional government and defense space agencies. Day to day, a satellite systems engineer might be designing the power subsystem for a smallsat constellation; a mission operations engineer might be managing a fleet of Earth observation satellites from a ground control center; a propulsion engineer might be testing a liquid rocket engine for a launch vehicle. The work demands rigorous engineering — space systems cannot be easily repaired.
keySkills: Designing satellite subsystems including power, communications, attitude determination, and thermal control
Applying orbital mechanics principles to mission design, launch window planning, and satellite operations
Programming flight software for embedded space systems under real-time constraints
Using spacecraft simulation tools for functional testing and mission planning
Operating satellite ground station systems and managing command and telemetry operations
Applying space systems engineering methodology across subsystems integration and verification
Testing space hardware under simulated environmental conditions including vacuum and thermal cycling
opportunities: Spacecraft systems engineer at a smallsat manufacturer or constellation operator
Mission operations engineer managing satellite health and operations
Propulsion engineer at a commercial launch vehicle development company
Ground systems engineer at a satellite communications company
Space software engineer developing flight or ground control software
Remote sensing data analyst at an Earth observation company
verificationNote: Space technology roles often require security clearance and may be subject to export control regulations; requirements vary by country and specific role.

journeyPhases.name: Fit and Admission Preparation
journeyPhases.focus: Research aerospace engineering, electrical engineering, or physics degree programs with space applications. Build awareness of the commercial space ecosystem and the specific engineering disciplines most relevant to your interests: systems, propulsion, software, or operations.

journeyPhases.name: Degree Study
journeyPhases.focus: Study the relevant engineering fundamentals while developing specialization in spacecraft systems, orbital mechanics, or space software. Pursue placements with space agencies, satellite companies, or launch startups — these are intensely competitive but transformative.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Target graduate roles at smallsat companies, launch vehicle startups, or established aerospace primes with space divisions. CubeSat university projects and hackathons provide experience and industry visibility. Security clearance eligibility is a practical requirement for government-adjacent roles.

title: Human-Computer Interaction (HCI)
summary: Research how people interact with technology and design systems that work with human cognition instead of against it. The foundational discipline behind every digital product that actually makes sense to use.
description: Human-computer interaction (HCI) professionals study the relationship between people and the digital and physical systems they use — applying cognitive science, psychology, ergonomics, and design thinking to understand and improve how humans and technology interact. HCI sits between computer science and behavioral science, producing both applied research findings and practical design guidelines that shape every digital product. At the research end, HCI scientists study eye movement patterns, cognitive workload, and decision-making in technology contexts. At the applied end, HCI practitioners design accessible systems, conduct usability evaluations, and define interaction standards for complex products. The growing integration of AI into everyday systems has made HCI research — especially around explainability, trust, and failure modes — more consequential than ever.
keySkills: Designing and conducting controlled user studies to evaluate interface usability and cognitive load
Applying cognitive psychology principles including mental models, attention, and working memory to design
Conducting accessibility evaluations using WCAG standards and assistive technology testing
Prototyping interaction concepts at different fidelities from paper to high-fidelity digital
Analyzing qualitative and quantitative user research data to generate actionable insights
Writing HCI research papers and presenting findings to both academic and practitioner audiences
Applying interaction design patterns and usability heuristics across web, mobile, and novel interfaces
opportunities: UX researcher with an HCI specialization at a large technology company
Human factors engineer at an aerospace, automotive, or medical device company
Accessibility specialist ensuring digital products meet WCAG and disability inclusion standards
HCI research scientist at a university lab or corporate research organization
Conversational UI designer applying HCI principles to voice and AI interactions
Game UX researcher applying HCI methods to improve player experience and onboarding

journeyPhases.name: Foundation
journeyPhases.focus: Study the fundamentals of cognitive psychology and how they apply to interface design. Read foundational HCI texts (Norman's The Design of Everyday Things is the standard starting point). Learn usability evaluation methods.

journeyPhases.name: Core Skills
journeyPhases.focus: Conduct real user studies — even small-scale projects develop the skill quickly. Learn to prototype interactions, run usability tests, and analyze both quantitative and qualitative data from user research sessions.

journeyPhases.name: Entry Transition
journeyPhases.focus: Build a research portfolio documenting study design, findings, and product impact. Target UX researcher roles at large technology companies, human factors roles at safety-critical industries, or HCI PhD programs for research-focused careers.
